HUNT.IO UNCOVERS RUSSIAN-SPEAKING CREDENTIAL THEFT OPERATION TARGETING US BANKS AND GOVERNMENT ACCOUNTS
Pierluigi Paganini

November 20, 2026
Hunt.io uncovered a credential-stealing operation that compromised 603 PCs and exposed bank, government and password manager accounts.

Hunt.io found an exposed open directory sitting on a Netherlands VPS, and inside it was the live loot store of a credential-theft operation. The report describes decrypted password-manager vaults, cleartext bank logins, and accounts behind the federal identity gateways ID.me and Login.gov. No bank or agency was breached directly; this all happened on the victims’ own Windows PCs.

The attackers used three custom-built tools to manage the operation. HavoX handled communication with infected computers and ran commands, Phantom53 managed victims and tasks, while the Kraken Bridge connected the system to an external control panel.

HavoX used encrypted connections and hidden Python scripts to operate quietly. Phantom53 tracked infected devices, while Kraken Bridge sent commands and delivered tasks through temporary download links that were deleted after use.

The operation affected 603 computers, which had been communicating with three command-and-control systems since October 12. In just three weeks, they generated more than 1.2 million connections. At least 57 victims had US bank or government login details stored on their computers, while 46 had accounts linked to federal benefits or identity services. In one case, the attacker cracked an entire LastPass vault offline, recovering 2,880 logins, including access to a bank account, the IRS and the vault’s own sharing key.

The attacker also bypassed Chrome’s newer app-bound encryption by using hardcoded AES-GCM keys for Chrome versions 20 and 21. A script then searched stolen cookies for 28 valuable […]

title: CVE-2026-123890: Critical VMware vCenter Zero-Day Exploited by China-Linked Hackers
text:
Broadcom has released emergency security updates addressing CVE-2026-123890, a critical authentication bypass vulnerability in VMware vCenter Server that was exploited as a zero-day by a suspected China-nexus cyberespionage actor. The flaw resides in the VMware Directory Service and carries a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8, Critical.

Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant attributed observed exploitation to ARMORY CASTLE, formerly tracked as UNC5221 and also known as Warp Panda. Forensic evidence indicates that the group exploited the vulnerability in early September 2026, more than two months before Broadcom publicly disclosed and patched it on November 19.

The attackers used a custom Golang exploitation utility named BONESAW to target VMware vCenter. Successful exploitation enabled the threat actor to establish an authenticated session as administrator@vsphere.local, extract the vCenter Lightning Memory-Mapped Database (LMDB), obtain SAML signing material, create rogue SSO administrator accounts, and execute commands on the affected appliance.

Contact Sales

The vulnerability is particularly dangerous because vCenter functions as the centralized control plane for VMware virtual infrastructure. Compromise can provide attackers with privileged access not only to the management appliance but potentially to managed ESXi hosts and virtual machines. In the observed intrusion, ARMORY CASTLE eventually accessed an ESXi host and extracted files from a Windows guest VM.

Organizations can strengthen defenses against emerging vulnerabilities with SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform, helping security teams operationalize threat intelligence and accelerate threat hunting and detection engineering across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments.

Security professionals can also use Prime Architect to transform emerging vulnerability intelligence into detection logic, generate hunting queries, and adapt behavioral detections to their organization’s available telemetry.

Detect CVE-2026-123890 by monitoring access to vCenter management services, especially TCP port 2012, alongside suspicious SSO account creation, unexpected administrative sessions, unusual use of the VAMI API, changes to SSH settings, and abnormal file or database access originating from vCenter.

CVE-2026-123890 analysis

CVE-2026-123890 affects VMware vCenter Server and related VMware Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation, and Telco Cloud environments. Broadcom classifies the issue as an authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service and assigns it the maximum Critical rating of 9.8 under CVSS 3.1.

Mandiant’s technical analysis provides considerably more detail about the underlying weakness. The vulnerability is an unauthenticated Secure Remote Password (SRP-6a) session-key disclosure issue reachable through Distributed Computing Environment/Remote Procedure Calls (DCE/RPC) handled by the vCenter Directory Service, or vmdird.

The relevant interface is exposed over TCP port 2012, which vCenter uses as a control interface for Single Sign-On functionality. ARMORY CASTLE specifically scanned internal environments for VMware-related services on ports including 443, 2012, 5480, and 9080 before exploiting vCenter.

The flaw involves VMware’s rpc_srp_verifier service. According to GTIG, weaknesses in cryptographic logic and authorization can expose a shared SRP session key. An attacker can then use this information to establish an authenticated session as:

administrator@vsphere.local

No valid administrator password is required.

Once the authenticated session is established, the attacker can interact with privileged VMware Directory Service interfaces. Mandiant states that an attacker can execute arbitrary commands and acquire files, including the underlying data.mdb database through the vmdirdbcp RPC interface.

BONESAW significantly automated these capabilities. Mandiant observed the tool being used to:

create a new SSO administrator […]

title: CVE-2026-126714: phpAfterShell PHP Session Flaw Can Lead to Remote Code Execution
text:
The PHP development team has released security updates addressing CVE-2026-126714, a critical vulnerability dubbed phpAfterShell that can turn partially overwritten session files into an arbitrary deserialization primitive and potentially remote code execution. The flaw carries a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2, Critical and affects PHP applications using the default file-based session handler.

Unlike a vulnerability confined to one CMS or framework, phpAfterShell exists in PHP itself. Applications built with WordPress, Laravel, custom PHP frameworks, or other software can therefore fall within the exposure scope if they run a vulnerable PHP release and store sessions as files. Applications using Redis, databases, or other non-file session handlers are outside this specific defect.

The vulnerability stems from how PHP updates existing session files. If an update is interrupted at the right moment, part of the new session data can overwrite the beginning of the file while bytes from the previous session remain at the end. PHP may later interpret this hybrid file as valid session state and deserialize attacker-controlled objects when the application calls session_start().

Successful exploitation requires several conditions, including attacker influence over session data, an interruption at a useful point during the write, and a suitable deserialization path. Depthfirst demonstrated that the primitive could be chained with a separate PHP-native memory-corruption technique to achieve code execution inside the PHP worker process.

Contact Sales

The issue is especially relevant because PHP’s session upload-progress feature can modify a session while PHP is still parsing an unauthenticated multipart request, before application code begins executing. This can give an attacker a pre-authentication path to manipulate file-backed session state under vulnerable configurations.

Organizations can use SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform to operationalize vulnerability intelligence and accelerate hunting for exploitation behavior across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments.

Detect CVE-2026-126714 by correlating suspicious multipart uploads, abnormal PHP session behavior, repeated worker crashes, and unexpected operating-system activity originating from PHP-FPM, Apache, or other PHP worker processes.

CVE-2026-126714 analysis

CVE-2026-126714 affects supported PHP branches prior to 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, and 8.5.13 when applications use file-backed sessions. PHP 8.6.0 was released with the correction included. Older PHP 8.1 and earlier releases are end-of-life and should be migrated to a supported branch rather than relied upon for ongoing security updates.

The vulnerability is located in PHP’s default files session save handler:

session.save_handler = files

PHP stores each session in a file such as:

<session.save_path>/sess_<SESSION_ID>

When session data changes, PHP serializes the new state and writes it into the existing file. The vulnerable design did not treat this update as a fully atomic transaction.

Under the default PHP session serialization format, multiple values are stored consecutively as records consisting of a session key and serialized value. Serialized strings contain explicit length information that tells PHP where a value ends and where parsing should continue.

That creates an important exploitation opportunity. Data that is harmless while positioned inside a serialized string can become active syntax when the beginning of the file is replaced with another carefully constructed session prefix.

Depthfirst researchers showed that two individually legitimate sessions could therefore be combined into a third valid but attacker-influenced session if the update process stops at the appropriate moment.

PHP writes the replacement session using filesystem operations such as pwrite() and ftruncate(). These operations are not guaranteed to behave as one atomic session commit. If the worker process […]

title: CVE-2026-132825: Ruby2Shell Heap Overflow Can Lead to Remote Code Execution
text:
En

CVEs

November 20, 2026
8 min read

Ruby maintainers have released security updates addressing CVE-2026-132825, a memory-corruption vulnerability dubbed Ruby2Shell that affects string case conversion in the Ruby interpreter. The issue is a one-byte heap-based buffer overflow that can be triggered when Ruby changes the case of specially crafted strings in certain legacy single-byte encodings, including ISO-8859-1 and Windows-1252.

The Ruby project rates the underlying GitHub Security Advisory as Critical and states that proofs of concept have demonstrated remote code execution in some scenarios. The published CVE record currently carries a CVSS 3.1 score of 7.4, High, reflecting a narrower exploitability assessment. This distinction matters: the memory corruption is confirmed, but practical remote exploitation depends on how an application accepts and processes attacker-controlled strings.

The flaw was patched alongside six additional vulnerabilities in Ruby’s regular expression engine and string-conversion logic. Fixed releases are Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13, and 4.0.10. Ruby 3.2 and earlier have reached end of life and will not receive upstream fixes.

Contact Sales

Ruby is embedded throughout modern web and developer infrastructure. Rails applications, classic-style Sinatra deployments, and self-hosted products that bundle Ruby can therefore inherit the flaw even when their own application code has not changed. Veria Labs says it independently demonstrated unauthenticated RCE against stock Rails.

Organizations can use SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform to operationalize emerging vulnerability intelligence and accelerate threat hunting across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments.

Detect CVE-2026-132825 by correlating suspicious legacy-encoded HTTP input with Ruby process crashes, memory-corruption events, and unexpected child-process or network activity originating from web application workers.

CVE-2026-132825 analysis

CVE-2026-132825 affects Ruby releases before 3.3.14, 3.4.13, and 4.0.10. The vulnerable code has existed since Ruby 2.4.0, meaning unsupported Ruby branches can also contain the bug even though they are no longer receiving upstream security fixes.

The root cause lies in Ruby’s case-conversion implementation for several legacy single-byte character encodings. In these encodings, the German sharp s character, ß, can expand from one byte of input into two output characters, SS, during uppercasing.

The vulnerable conversion loop verifies that there is room for one byte in the destination buffer, writes the first S, and later writes the second S without performing another bounds check. Ruby allocates the output buffer with limited additional space, so carefully sized input containing enough expansion characters can cause the final byte to be written just beyond the allocated heap region.

Veria Labs reports that an input containing 21 sharp-s characters can cross the buffer boundary and create the one-byte overwrite. The affected path is reachable through methods including upcase, swapcase, downcase(:fold), and casecmp?. UTF-8 strings follow a different code path and are not affected by this specific vulnerability.

The size of the primitive is small but still security-relevant. A one-byte heap overwrite can corrupt adjacent heap metadata or nearby objects, and the converted result can also lead to an out-of-bounds read. Whether this becomes RCE depends heavily on the memory allocator, process layout, target application, Ruby version, surrounding heap objects, and the attacker’s ability to repeatedly shape memory.

Veria Labs likewise states that Rails and classic-style Sinatra are exposed by default on affected Ruby releases, while plain Rack and other frameworks are not necessarily exposed unless application code performs the relevant case conversion on attacker-controlled data. A vulnerable Ruby runtime therefore does not automatically prove that every application running on it is […]

title: CVE-2026-120382: Critical Synology DSM OAuth Flaw Enables Arbitrary File Access
text:
Synology has disclosed a critical vulnerability affecting DiskStation Manager (DSM) and BeeStation OS that can allow unauthenticated remote attackers to read or write arbitrary files and trigger denial-of-service conditions. Tracked as CVE-2026-120382, the flaw resides in the OAuth API and carries a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8, Critical.

The vulnerability is classified as CWE-88: Improper Neutralization of Argument Delimiters in a Command. According to Synology, the affected OAuth API fails to properly neutralize command argument delimiters, allowing attacker-controlled input to alter how a downstream command interprets its parameters. No authentication or user interaction is required.

The issue is particularly serious for organizations exposing Synology NAS management services to untrusted networks. Successful exploitation could expose confidential files stored on the NAS, allow attackers to modify or replace files, or disrupt device availability. Synology’s official advisory does not currently state that the vulnerability directly enables arbitrary command execution or remote code execution, so the confirmed impact should be limited to the vendor-documented file read/write and denial-of-service capabilities.

Contact Sales

The vulnerability affects multiple DSM generations as well as BeeStation OS 1.5. Synology recommends updating supported installations as soon as fixed builds become available and deactivating the OAuth Service package as an immediate workaround. As of November 20, 2026, the advisory remains marked Ongoing, with fixes for several affected product branches still in progress.

Organizations can use SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform to operationalize emerging vulnerability intelligence and accelerate threat hunting and detection engineering across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments.

Detect CVE-2026-120382 by correlating suspicious access to Synology authentication and OAuth functionality with unexpected file-system activity, unusual DSM service behavior, repeated service failures, and anomalous outbound connections from NAS devices.

CVE-2026-120382 analysis

CVE-2026-120382 affects Synology DiskStation Manager releases across several major branches. Synology’s detailed advisory lists vulnerable versions before DSM 6.2.4-25556-9, 7.1.1-42962-10, 7.2.1-69057-14, 7.2.2-72806-11, 7.3.2-86009-6, and 7.4.1-90080-2.

The current product matrix specifically marks the following supported products as affected:

ProductStatusFixed release / recommendationBeeStation OS 1.5CriticalFix ongoingDSM 7.4CriticalUpgrade to 7.4.1-90080-2 or laterDSM 7.3CriticalUpgrade to 7.3.2-86009-6 or laterDSM 7.2.2CriticalFix ongoing; upgrade to 7.3.2-86009-6+ recommendedDSM 7.2.1CriticalFix ongoing; upgrade to 7.3.2-86009-6+ recommendedDSM 7.1CriticalFix ongoingAPM 1.2 / 2.0Not affectedNo action for this CVEDSM Enterprise 1.0Not affectedNo action for this CVESRM 1.2 / 1.3Not affectedNo action for this CVE

An important detail is that DSM 6.2 does not appear in Synology’s current affected-products table, but the technical version description explicitly identifies versions before DSM 6.2.4-25556-9 as vulnerable. Organizations maintaining older or end-of-life NAS systems should therefore verify the installed build instead of assuming that absence from the current support matrix means the system is safe.

The root cause involves improper handling of command argument delimiters inside the OAuth API. Argument injection differs from traditional OS command injection: rather than necessarily inserting an entirely new shell command, an attacker manipulates the arguments supplied to a legitimate backend command so it performs operations that were not intended by the application.

title: Kirsten Davies's White House Promotion Leaves CMMC in Limbo
text:
Government
,
Industry Specific

Standards, Regulations & Compliance

Kirsten Davies's White House Promotion Leaves CMMC in Limbo
Sean Cairncross Ejected from National Cyber Director Position

Shaun Waterman •
November 20, 2026

$('.fa.fa-print').click(function () {
window.print();
});

Image: Shutterstock

The replacement of National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross by Department of Defense CIO Kirsten Davies may be good for the NCD post and the nation, but doesn't bode as well for the troubled Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification program that she is leaving behind at the Pentagon, an expert and former officials tell ISMG.See Also: How 'Radical Transparency' Can Bolster Cybersecurity
It was hard to see any wins or real achievements during Cairncross' relatively brief 15 months in the post, said one career official who served in senior cybersecurity positions in DHS under Republican and Democratic administrations. The five-page national cybersecurity strategy released in March, was "a punchline," this former official said.
"A strategy is meant to be high level, but this could, if you're being charitable, be described as too high level, or just slogans It didn't contain enough of a defined vision to be turned into an implementation plan (see: Trump's National Cyber Strategy Leaves Industry Role Unclear).
Setting the national strategy document aside, the former official added, "there still was ample room to do some more ambitious projects, and we didn't really see that coming out of the White House."
Cairncross, a GOP political operative with no substantial cybersecurity background or technical skills, couldn't even deliver when it came to his supposed stock-in-trade, political infighting and horse-trading within the administration, the former official said.
"He was hamstrung by the political football of who owns AI security," which resulted in Cairncross' office being sidelined. "The pitch for him was that OK, he lacked [cybersecurity] experience, but he was a smooth political operator and he had the ear of the president. And I think the failure to turn that into leadership on an issue as important as AI security means that that one benefit he was supposed to bring to the table he didn't actually bring."
The whole point of the NCD's office was to be a hub of subject matter expertise in the White House that could coordinate interagency policy, "And it was more important than ever given the diminished role of CISA. I don't think he succeeded in building that," the official said.
On the other hand, the official added, Davies has nearly two decades in technology and cybersecurity executive jobs for large enterprises in technology, finance and other sectors, culminating in her role as CISO for Unilever, one of the world’s largest household goods companies.
"I don't know many people who wouldn't say that she's quite capable," the official said. "The CIO position at the Pentagon is a very challenging role because it requires demonstrating leadership without extensive authorities over the DOD bureaucracy. I think she's done a decent job of figuring out, this is where we can make real improvements. This is what we can fight for."
Picking your battles and carefully setting priorities were key skills for a senior White House official like the NCD. "I think Davies already has an appreciation of what's possible and what can be gained by bringing senior White House attention to a project. … I think she has the experience to be able to pick and choose. This is what we need to lean in on. This is what's possible. This is what will be a stretch, but it's worth fighting for," the former official said.
Those comments were echoed by Joshua Marpet, a freelance cybersecurity consultant who volunteered as a member of one of the working groups that helped develop CMMC in 2019-20.

title: House Lawmakers Push US AI Models to Counter China
text:
Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning
,

House Lawmakers Push US AI Models to Counter China
Congressional Report Urges Federal Open-Weight AI Initiative as Chinese Models Gain Ground in US Firms

Emilia David •
November 20, 2026

$('.fa.fa-print').click(function () {
window.print();
});

Image: Shutterstock/ISMG

House lawmakers recommended Friday that the Trump administration establish an initiative for American-made open-weight AI models that would entice organizations to turn away from Chinese open-weight models.See Also: 43% Are Piloting Healthcare AI Agents. Just 3% Have Deployed Them

The House Select Committee on China published a report focusing on how widespread Chinese open-weight models such as DeepSeek, Kimi, Qwen, and GLM are. The report is based on an investigation begun in April into why three American companies, Airbnb, Anysphere, Cursor and DoorDash, turned to these models.

The committee found that Chinese models are widely used in the economy, "but much of that use is hard to track." Most organizations using these models cite their low cost, easy customization and performance as key drivers.

The lawmakers said in the report that "risks are increasing" with Chinese models producing less secure code and autonomously building cyber exploits, so the government must encourage the creation of U.S. open-weight models.

The committee proposes several measures, including launching a national American open-weight AI initiative "that pairs public compute, shared evaluation infrastructure and lawful access to American frontier models for training with anchor demand from federal procurement.
The White House should also prohibit federal agencies from using Chinese models and the government should subject the models to consistent evaluation, lawmakers said. They also recommended sanctioning companies that illicitly distill U.S.-made models.

Before the committee released its findings, CNBC reported that Cursor, which SpaceX recently bought, plans to stop using Chinese models. The company built its coding model Composer 2 using Kimi K2.5 from Chinese AI lab Moonshot AI.

The most popular American-made models, those from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, are all proprietary models, meaning these companies are not required to share the weights of their models or release any detailed training information. Open-weight models often don't share training data, but their makers do provide weights, allowing users to customize parts of the model. These models often cost a fraction of closed models.

Some American open-weight models do exist. Meta's Llama and Muse models have always operated under an open-source license and are considered open-weight. Nvidia, long an advocate for open-source AI, distributes the open-weight Nemotron. OpenAI and Google also have open-weight models, oss and Gemma, respectively.

Proponents of proprietary models believe that open-weight models are not as capable as their proprietary counterparts and are less secure. Many experts told ISMG that open-weight models, particularly those from Chinese labs, are steadily closing in on frontier models. The House committee also noted this increase in capability and warned that many safety evaluations may not detect certain behavior from these models.

One reason Chinese open-weight models are developing quickly may be due to distillation, where developers prompt a teacher model like Claude Fable and use its responses and reasoning chains as training data for their own models. Such practice is accepted in some research cases, but the U.S. government, citing information from Anthropic and OpenAI, said many Chinese labs do so without permission and illicitly.

Vineet Edupuganti, co-founder and CEO, Cogent Security (Image: Cogent Security)

Cogent plans to purchase an AI security startup led by an ex-CrowdStrike manager to help customers identify which vulnerabilities and misconfigurations should be prioritized.See Also: NodeZero® for Pentesters and Red Teams
The San Francisco-based autonomous cyber defense platform said its proposed acquisition of San Francisco-based Specular will make it easier for customers to do outside-in attack-path analysis, exploitability assessment and validation of remediation work, said co-founder and CEO Vineet Edupuganti. Specular's external view will complement Cogent's existing inside-out analysis, he said.
"One of the top questions that people are asking, especially in this age of frontier AI and heightened vulnerabilities and exploits of those vulnerabilities, is just, 'What is actually exploitable?'" Edupuganti told ISMG. "People have so many different findings in their ecosystem, and so, 'What is a small subset that can actually lead to a breach?'"
Specular, founded in August 2024, employs fewer than five people and closed a seed investment round in July 2025. The company has been led since its inception by Peyton Smith, who spent more five years at CrowdStrike, culminating in a role as manager of red team services. Prior to that, he spent two-and-a-half years as a threat researcher and information security analyst at Anomali (see: Cogent Security Gets $42M to Boost AI Vulnerability Defense).
Validating Whether Vulnerabilities Can Lead to Exploitation
Organizations face many vulnerability findings, but only a subset may realistically lead to a breach. Edupuganti said Cogent's existing inside-out attack-path analysis, combined with Specular's outside-in view of an environment, will help customers identify which issues deserve priority. Specular's team brings professional red-team experience and built its product from an attacker's perspective.
"What Specular brings is a very good complement," Edupuganti said. "It's this outside-in aspect where they can see the environment from the outside, the way that an attacker would. That, joined with what we've already built, is extremely powerful. It allows us to give customers a really good sense of, 'Given all my vulnerabilities, here's a small subset of those that you really want to focus on.'"
Specular's AI-based engine validates whether vulnerabilities can lead to exploitation, addressing the false positives and noise that can burden security teams. Combining Specular with Cogent's contextual information about assets, business relationships, and controls can help map how an attacker might move through an environment and identify which risks are most likely to lead to a breach, he said.
"These are professional red teamers who have spent years hacking into the world's biggest companies, and so they built the company and the product with that perspective in mind," Edupuganti said. "What they're able to bring is this AI layer that has very good in-built validation, and it also can probe and understand if a vulnerability can truly lead to exploitation activity."
Determining whether a vulnerability is exploitable helps customers decide what to address first, Edupuganti said. Issues that do not appear exploitable may be deferred, while exploitable issues - especially those exposed at the edge - may require immediate attention. After a customer fixes a vulnerability, Edupuganti said Specular's scanning can help confirm whether it is still present.

title: Google Builds Fake Internet to Test AI Agent Security
text:
Agentic AI
,
Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning
,

Google Builds Fake Internet to Test AI Agent Security
Mirror Dimension' Tests Chrome Agents Against Prompt Injection Without Alerting Them

Emilia David •
November 20, 2026

$('.fa.fa-print').click(function () {
window.print();
});

Image: Shutterstock

Google wanted to observe how browser-use agents behave in realistic settings, but the agents knew they were being tested.See Also: Secure AI Everywhere

So, to ensure the agents don't realize they're being tested, Google researchers built a "mirror dimension," a synthetic environment that mimics the real internet.

"This controlled testing ground lets engineers evaluate auto browse in realistic online environments, featuring thousands of simulated websites inspired by everyday user journeys, without creating real-world security risks," the researchers said in a blog post.

Browser-use agents can be targets for scams and security breaches, which can be especially dangerous when agents carry sensitive information on behalf of their users. These agents can also visit websites and download information or access user accounts.

Google added browser-use agents, or "auto browse," to Chrome in January. The company billed it as a way to save time on tedious forms, vacation research or appointment scheduling. Users can direct these agents to popular websites, often without providing a URL, so the agent must infer which website they mean. Because the internet is always changing, Google said it would be ineffective and irresponsible to throw agents to the real web during testing. The Mirror Dimension environment provides a safe, reliable, and repeatable place to observe agents.

The Mirror Dimension is a mix of an isolated sandbox that houses realistic fake websites and a "local interception proxy," effectively a middleman that stands in for the agent's real destination.
The first problem propelling Google was evaluation awareness, or when AI models and agents realize they are being tested. This is a growing problem that many frontier AI labs say makes it difficult to trust tests. Simply telling the agent to navigate to a fake URL "easily breaks the realism of the eval and induces eval awareness."

To avoid this, Google developed a way for the agent to navigate to the real URL - for example, www.youtube.com - but the agent taps a headless Chrome browser that prevents the agent's request from reaching the external DNS and loads the fake website instead. Chrome normally blocks this type of action to protect users.

The interception proxy creates certificates that the agents are told to accept to gain access to the fake website. Google said this approach is safe because hackers need to have full administrator control over a computer before starting the process.

Once the agent reached the synthetic site, Google began testing whether it could be tricked into misbehaving. The researchers planted malicious instructions in different parts of the fake website, such as in the visible text, inside images, in the underlying code or in hidden descriptions for screen readers. Through this, they can observe whether the agent follows its original instructions and reads the website or fills in forms without taking bad directions.

Google said this process removes the bottleneck of security engineers being unable to verify realistic attacks when they design hand-crafted evaluations for browser-use agents.

"Our automated red-teaming pipeline uses the 'mirror dimension' to test and refine our engineers' ideas across a variety of sites," Google said. "That frees our experts to focus on discovering new attack techniques while the pipeline handles the repetitive work of refinement and evaluation."

Some enterprises have been experimenting with computer-use agents to build a hybrid human-and-agent workflow. But these agents aren't available in all browsers, and they can be expensive; new methods are […]

title: Japan's week in cybersecurity, Nov 15–21.One breached platform, KARTE, put seven companies on our list of 2026's largest breaches, now 78: DHC, JINS, Shimamura, GDO, Francfranc, RIZAP, Club Tourism.Also: Rakuten Securities' test environment, a second GSS breach at the Digital Agency, 233 passphrase-less keys taken from Fugaku, payment platforms behind other apps, and new PHP, Java and Ruby flaws.https://japancyberwatch.com/articles/japan-cyber-week-2026-11-21#infosec #Japan
text:
The week one platform filled the list. Our list of 2026's largest breaches grew from 68 to 78, and seven of the ten new entries came from a single breach: KARTE, a customer platform that hundreds of Japanese companies feed with their members' data. Rakuten Securities found millions of customers' bank accounts and incomes in a test environment. The Digital Agency reported a second breach of GSS, the government's own IT platform. RIKEN counted the keys taken from Fugaku. And new flaws in PHP, Java and Ruby kept administrators busy.
The week in numbers

These figures overlap and mix records with people, so they cannot simply be added up. Two earlier entries changed: Nojima rose to 7.18 million after a second site was found, and the hotel system Temairazu cut its estimate from up to 4.45 million to about 1 million in its final report.
KARTE: one breach, seven names on the list#
PLAID's KARTE has been stopped since November 13. This week its customers started counting: DHC, JINS, Shimamura, Golf Digest Online, Francfranc with Ain Holdings' cosmetics stores, RIZAP and Club Tourism all reported millions of records, mostly birth dates, genders, email addresses and member IDs rather than full profiles.
On November 20, PLAID published its findings. A flaw in part of a public route used to fetch data let the attackers take credentials and log in to the admin screen. Integration credentials of 754 customer companies leaked, and imported data of 570; analytics data of 487 and cache data of up to 409 are also affected. The data of companies whose contracts had ended was there too, kept by mistake. KARTE will restart in stages from mid-January 2027, and PLAID cut its forecast for the year from a ¥1.6 billion operating profit to a ¥0.9 billion loss. PLAID gives customers detailed data from November 24, so more notices are likely.
The other new names on the list#

Rakuten Securities: data in a system in its test environment may have been taken on November 11: login IDs for up to 11.25 million accounts and, for up to 4.47 million, names, addresses, employers, withdrawal bank accounts, self-reported income and assets and holdings. Its logins are protected by passkeys. The data was somewhere else.
GoQSystem, an order management service for shops selling on several online malls, says a flaw in an inquiry form let attackers take 4.98 million orders of 1,694 shops' customers. Shops can join a single report to the privacy regulator until November 26.
Yeny, which runs prepaid card and sports team payment apps, says a misconfigured API connection leaked 1.33 million phone numbers and member IDs.

Platforms behind other companies' apps#
KARTE was not the only shared platform. Infcurion's Wallet Station, which powers other companies' payment apps and regional points, was accessed on the night of November 19; up to about 250,000 records leaked, including passwords and bank account details. Infcurion has not named the providers and is inspecting all of […]

Two are in products we have already covered, Cisco Expressway and VMware vCenter. The other two are less well known and more awkward than they look: an unauthenticated code-execution flaw in Apache Roller, where the obvious workaround does not work, and a flaw in SAP NetWeaver Enterprise Portal that SAP rated only medium a year ago and that CISA now says is being used in attacks.
The Monday date is a US federal rule and not a UK obligation. We are using it here as a prompt: a Friday evening list with a Monday date is a reasonable way to decide what gets looked at first this weekend.
#Apache Roller: switching off XML-RPC in the admin screen is not enough
Apache Roller is an open-source blogging server written in Java. The flaw, CVE-2026-129448, is scored 9.8 out of 10, and the Apache Software Foundation’s own text in the CVE record says it “is being actively exploited”. According to that record, versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4 contain a deserialisation flaw in the XML-RPC endpoint: the endpoint accepts “vendor extension types” and unpacks them before it has checked who is asking. An attacker needs no account, only network access to the endpoint, and can run arbitrary code on the server.
The detail that matters most to anyone running Roller is in the workaround Apache gives. Apache says users who cannot upgrade straight away should set “enabledForExtensions” to “false” in WEB-INF/web.xml, or remove the “/roller-services/xmlrpc” servlet mapping, and then restart Roller. It adds that disabling XML-RPC in the administration screen is not enough, because older versions deserialise the request before they check that setting. We would expect plenty of […]

The flaw, CVE-2026-123890, is in the VMware Directory Service and carries a CVSS score of 9.8, according to The Hacker News’s report on the advisory. Broadcom’s advisory does not mention attacks, lists no workaround, and says the issue “qualifies under ITIL methodologies as an emergency change”. Fixed versions exist for every supported branch.
Updated Friday 20 November, 21:10 UK time: CISA has now added CVE-2026-123890 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue, with a federal due date of Monday 23 November. See “CISA’s listing, and what it changes” below.
Earlier update, Friday 20 November, UK time: Google’s Mandiant team says a suspected Chinese espionage group was already exploiting this flaw as a zero-day, meaning before any patch existed, from early September, and that is not in Broadcom’s advisory. We have rewritten this story to reflect it, and the section “Google says it was used for more than two months before the patch” has the details. Broadcom also reissued the advisory on 20 November (version 9.1) to clarify the affected VMware Tools versions. Treat any vCenter that was reachable on your network as possibly compromised until you have checked, as well as unpatched.
#What the advisory covers
The advisory has five entries, and only one of them is the headline. CVE-2026-123890 is the vCenter authentication bypass. The other four are lower-rated: an SQL injection (CVE-2026-123891), an authenticated command injection (CVE-2026-123892) and a local privilege escalation (CVE-2026-123893), all in SDDC Manager, plus a SAML token signature bypass in VMware Tools for Windows (CVE-2026-123894). title: 🤖 Bazuka: new Android malware framework found by ThreatFabric while investigating an NFC-relay banking trojan. Fake screen overlays hide credential theft and on-device control, and an LLM integration is used for victim management at scale. 🔗 https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/bazuka-android-malware-uses-fake-screen.html #Malware #Android #CyberSec #InfoSec
text:
Bazuka Android Malware Uses Fake Screen Overlays to Hide Credential Theft and Device ControlRavie LakshmananNov 20, 2026Mobile Security / Artificial Intelligence

//<![CDATA[
document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded",()=>{let t=document.querySelector("h1.story-title"),m=document.querySelector(".postmeta");t&&m&&t.insertAdjacentElement("afterend",m)})
//]]>

Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a previously unknown Android malware framework called Bazuka that offers large language model (LLM) integration for victim management and control at scale.

Dutch mobile security company ThreatFabric said it discovered the threat in late October 2026 during an investigation into an NFC-relay banking Trojan.

"Bazuka is a full malware framework," ThreatFabric said in a technical report. "A dropper/downloader, a core, and 23 modules cover overlays, keylogging, 2FA and SMS interception, remote control, and crypto-address swapping."

One notable aspect of the malware that distinguishes it from the rest is a novel overlay technique that allows the trojan to take a screenshot of the home screen or lock screen, and display that as an overlay on demand to cover up malicious activities taking place in the background.

Another perhaps not-so-surprising element is the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in the control panel to help operators identify victims of interest and manage infections. It supports both locally hosted models and models accessed through an API.

One of the sample prompts provided by the author refers to a score, indicating an operator can likely request the AI model to score victims and determine how attractive they are as targets. The panel also supports the following capabilities -

Create accounts for traffers, who are cybercriminals responsible for driving victims to malware using various lures
Build droppers containing the malware with options to choose the kind of permissions specified in the Android manifest file likely in an attempt to bypass Google Play app review process

This indicates that the dropper apps can be distributed via at least two distribution channels: through traffers, who can use social media ads or bogus sites to trick users into downloading them, and Google Play Store.

One of the droppers containing the malware masquerades as a premium, adult-friendly version of TikTok (package name: "com.tiktok.premium"). Two different variants of the Bazuka attack chain have been observed -

A dropper, which asks the victim for permissions to install applications from third-party sources and then proceeds to download a standalone APK ("com.tiktok.premium.pro") that serves as the stager
A downloader that directly downloads the main payload

It's suspected that the stager is the same as the downloader, whose main responsibility is to retrieve the core and supplementary modules necessary for a particular campaign, and then launch them.

"Once the core and required modules are loaded, Bazuka operates as a keylogger and a classic overlay trojan, monitoring the text entered by the victim and displaying an overlay at the right moment," ThreatFabric said. "All functionality is controlled by commands from C2 [command-and-control]."

The core module is the orchestrator, maintaining communication with C2, loading additional DEX modules, dispatching commands, collecting device information, and managing permissions and component updates. Like other Android trojans, it abuses Android Debug Bridge (ADB) shell commands and the operating system's accessibility services to request permissions and grant them automatically.

"Important components of the core include mechanisms for enabling Wireless Debugging and completing the pairing process," ThreatFabric explained. "The core can open the system settings screen, find the relevant menu, enable Developer options, and then enable Wireless Debugging."

"When this mode is enabled, it also intercepts the PIN, which is then used to establish a TLS connection to the […]

Security Flaws in Mobile Switching, 2022 Report Warned
FOIA Suit Forces Release of 2022 Assessment Detailing Surveillance on US Carriers

Chris Riotta (@chrisriotta) •
November 20, 2026

$('.fa.fa-print').click(function () {
window.print();
});

Image: Shutterstock

A report commissioned in 2022 by the U.S. federal government depicted the state of mobile telecommunications security as riddled with holes exploited for espionage by foreign actors.See Also: Prioritize Preparation, Basics and Transparency, Experts Urge IRISSCON Attendees
The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has sought to keep the report away from the public - despite heavy pressure to publish it from U.S. Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., who made its release a condition for withdrawing procedural obstacles he set up stymieing the confirmation of Sean Plankey as CISA director. Plankey withdrew from consideration in April (see: Trump's Top Cyber Nominee Withdraws After Turbulent Process).
The Electronic Privacy Information Center published Thursday a redacted copy of the report after obtaining it in an open records lawsuit.
Report authors described a "perilous and untenable" situation created by foreign actors' ability to connect into a mobile routing system designed in the 1970s without much consideration for security.
The report lists the kinds of malicious traffic hitting U.S. networks, ranging from location tracking and call interception to phone hijacking and denial-of-service floods. The authors warn that without stronger defenses, "undefended U.S. telecoms networks constitute a vulnerable National Critical Function."
AdaptiveMobile Security prepared the assessment with under a Department of Homeland Security contract. Titled "U.S. Telecommunications Insecurity 2022," the review focuses on Signaling System 7, a decades-old protocol that carriers rely on to pass calls and texts to one another, as well as Diameter, the signaling standard behind 4G. The authors found that the industry's reliance on trust between operators had failed and urged a shift to zero trust.
The document describes surveillance activity detected on U.S. networks in early 2022. In March of that year, a phone in Indianapolis carrying a Cypriot subscriber identity received a location query sent through network addresses leased by a broker that the authors believe works for a nation-state agency. The report says the attempt likely succeeded due to a gap in the operator's defenses.

In late April, queries originating in Southeast Asia targeted three U.S. subscribers whose numbers the attackers appeared to already hold, which the authors said may suggest an earlier breach. They also tied the sending broker to surveillance-for-hire operations.

The authors logged more than 9,000 signaling violations against a single operator over seven days in May - including more than 2,000 in one 24-hour stretch. They believe the activity may have masked attempts to extract subscriber identities. AdaptiveMobile had warned the operator about that category of attack in 2019, according to the report.

The authors attributed much of the risk to the shape of the U.S. market, pointing to a patchwork of rural licenses that gives attackers numerous ways onto the signaling network, as well as domestic roaming traffic between carriers that often gets less scrutiny than traffic arriving from overseas. Some small carriers have rented network access to third parties that then appear on the signaling network as U.S. operators, and several companies profiled in the report run no active radio network at all.

The authors also found that some domestic roaming traffic could be carried through facilities in Canada and Germany and that one operator was sending such traffic through Switzerland and Italy. The Federal Communications Commission regulates how carriers handle customer network data but no framework governs […]

The ransomware group tracked as incransom has allegedly listed the Italian energy and utilities company Eni (eni.it) on its dark web leak site. According to the threat actor, the attack was purportedly carried out on 19 November 2026. The group claims to have exfiltrated approximately 18.78 GB of data spanning multiple categories, including contracts, finance and accounting records, procurement documents, legal materials, HR files, and confidential correspondence.
This report is based solely on the threat actor’s unverified leak site posting. Yazoul Security has not independently confirmed the breach, the authenticity of the data, or the accuracy of the claimed volume. Ransomware operators frequently inflate both the scope and sensitivity of stolen material to increase pressure on victims.
Threat Actor Profile
The group operating as incransom is a ransomware and data extortion operation. Public research on this specific actor remains limited, and its total number of known victims is not reliably documented. Its known tooling and tactics are not publicly characterized in available sources, which limits our ability to assess operational maturity or technical sophistication.
What can be said is that the group follows the established double extortion model: stealing data before or during encryption and threatening publication to coerce payment. The claimed attack date and the structured, category-by-category breakdown of data on the leak site are consistent with how extortion crews present material to maximize perceived impact. However, presentation style is not evidence of accuracy. Without a documented track record, credibility should be treated as unproven.
Alleged Data Exposure
According to the threat actor, the purported dataset includes:

Contracts and commercial relationships: allegedly 7,105 unique files (18.78 GB) covering signed contracts, customer and supplier agreements, service contracts, and agency agreements.
Finance and accounting: allegedly 28,562 files (1.91 GB) including invoices, payments, tax filings, balance sheets, and banking documents.
Public procurement and tenders: allegedly 3,041 files (1.13 GB) referencing CONSIP, ODA, tender documentation, and competitive bids.
Legal matters and litigation: allegedly 939 files (0.72 GB) covering claims, proceedings, and enforcement actions.
Due diligence and anti-corruption materials: purportedly relating to named counterparties, questionnaires, and screening records.
Personal data and HR: allegedly 1,092 HR files and 479 GDPR- and privacy-related files.
Confidential information: allegedly 570 files marked restricted, secret, or confidential.

These figures are the group’s own claims and have not been verified. The internal arithmetic of the stated categories does not fully reconcile, which is common in inflated leak site postings.
Potential Impact
If the claim is accurate, the exposure of finance, procurement, and legal records at a major energy firm could carry regulatory, contractual, and reputational consequences. The purported presence of HR and GDPR-related files would raise data protection obligations under Italian and EU law. Sector Watch

TP

The Perimeter Desk
Sector Watch

2026-11-20

# N0n Ransomware Gang Leaks Customer Data from Visa Mastercard and JPMorgan

If you're in a SOC and your first move is checking if Chase or Visa actually buckled, you've got the wrong map. You're staring at the front door while someone who doesn't even work there left the back window open.

The wire is a mess this week, and financial Services is where the real blood is. It sits at number three on the targeting list with 155 stories tracked over seven days. This isn't noise. It's a coordinated squeeze. The main act is the N0n ransomware gang, and they leaked customer data from JPMorgan, Visa, and Mastercard.

PR teams will start calling this "sophisticated. I hate that word. To me, it's just shorthand for saying they don't know how the attackers got in, but they want it to sound like an act of God so the board doesn't fire them, and these hits aren't cinematic heists. They are usually just boring failures.

In this case, it wasn't even a direct hit on the big banks. It was a third-party vendor compromise.

Blast radius is the only thing that really counts here. When you ship your data out to a vendor for "efficiency" or "specialized processing," you aren't moving the risk (you are, actually, just shifting the point of failure). You're handing it off to a company with a smaller security budget and likely a slower patching cycle; it's like giving your keys to someone living in a house with no locks and hoping for the best.

Take Rakuten Securities. They've been hit, and we are looking at millions of exposed customers. The exact number is still hovering around that "millions" mark, but the impact is binary: either your data is safe or it isn't. For a securities firm, the blast radius isn't just identity theft; it's market confidence.

Why finance? Why now? Because the payout is guaranteed and the leverage is absolute; encrypting a hospital means playing with lives (which is monstrous but unpredictable). Leaking customer lists from the world's largest payment rails threatens more than a company, and it threatens the plumbing of global commerce.

Defenders in this sector are fighting on two fronts, and they spend millions hardening their own cores, yet they remain tethered to thousands of smaller suppliers who treat security as a checkbox for compliance audits.

I saw this play out during NotPetya back in '17, and everyone remembers the global chaos and shipping ports freezing up. But the actual catalyst was a corrupted update from a tiny Ukrainian accounting package called M.E.Doc, and the sophistication wasn't in the exploit; it was in the trust, and maersk didn't fall because their firewalls were weak. They fell because they trusted software that had become a Trojan horse.

The parallel here is the supply chain; the difference is intent: NotPetya was a wiper (it wanted to destroy). N0n and these other crews want extort money. They don't want to burn the building down; they want to hold the blueprints for ransom while selling the guest list to the highest bidder.

Some of you will argue that third-party risk management (TPRM) handles this, and you'll cite questionnaires, SOC2 reports, and rigorous vendor audits.

That's a fantasy. A questionnaire is just a way for a vendor to lie to you in a format that looks professional. An audit is a snapshot of a single day in January, and it doesn't tell you if the vendor's admin forgot to rotate his password in July or left an RDP port open on a Friday afternoon. If you rely on a PDF report to ensure safety, you aren't managing risk; you're documenting your eventual failure.

Let's look at second-order effects, because that's where the real cost lives. It's not just about the "thousands" of customers whose names and emails are floating around on leak sites.

Insurance carriers feel it first. When one vendor breach takes down three or four global giants at […]

Free 30-day trial Data belonging to customers of three of the biggest companies in global finance has been leaked online, after hackers breached third-party service providers working for JPMorgan Chase, Visa, and Mastercard.The finance companies have all acknowledged that security incidents have occurred at unnamed third--party companies, after the n0n extortion gang named all three on its dark web leak site earlier this week.In JPMorgan Chase's case, it tweeted that although it believed "the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses" there had been "no disruption" to its services.

Mastercard also said that its payment network had not been affected, and that cardholders could continue to use their cards.According to Visa, the breach occurred at an unnamed third-party provider based in Asia Pacific.n0n claims to have stolen "hundreds of thousands of campaign interactions" related to JPMorgan Chase. All three of the corporations were given 48 hours to negotiate with the extortion gang, but none of them paid. So, n0n published data on its website exposing the details of thousands of customers.News of the security breach impacted the share prices of all three companies, after a jittery week of high-profile technology outages in the United States.According to Reuters, the leaked JPMorgan Chase data included more than 16,000 customer email addresses, and what appeared to be the email addresses of some 124 employees of the bank. Some of the customer information included phone numbers, and post codes.Clearly scammers and fraudsters could exploit information like that in a variety of ways, including by contacting members of the public claiming to be employees of their bank.Meanwhile, according to a Cybernews report, the leaked Visa data includes details of over 6000 premium card holders who are signed up to Asia-Pacific dining programmes, including names, phone numbers, the messaging apps they use, and restaurant booking details.n0n is believed to be a Russia-based extortion gang, and despite only having been operating for a couple of months has already managed to claim the scalps of approximately 200 corporate victims.Security researchers say n0n has typically broken into organisations using valid login credentials, harvested by info-stealing malware or obtained by credential-stuffing VPNs and poorly secured remote desktop (RDP) services, before using legitimate admin tools to gather data. It is not yet known how the vendors in this case were compromised.Of course, financial institutions are very experienced at securing their own infrastructure. Where they appear to have fallen down on this occasion is through the use of third-party marketing agencies or loyalty scheme operators who have been less diligent in securing their systems.You are only as safe as the weakest link in the chain. And customers don't really care whose server it was that leaked their data, when they entrusted it to your care in the first place.The advice for concerned Chase, Visa or Mastercard customers is simple: be wary of unexpected emails, texts or calls claiming to come from your bank. It would not be a surprise at all if scammers exploit the breach by mentioning it to customers, and offering compensation, or inviting members of the public to "verify" their account.If you are unsure, contact your bank directly using its published number. tags Industry News

text:
Image Credits:MirageC / Getty Images

Security

A transcription firm used by police, prosecutors, and tech giants exposed customer data online

Zack Whittaker

7:46 AM PST · November 20, 2026

A transcription company that caters to law enforcement, government departments, and Silicon Valley tech giants has resolved a security lapse after leaving a large amount of internal data, including customer transcriptions and their source materials, exposed to the web.

The data security lapse at San Francisco-based Tigerfish exposed transcriptions of police interviews, body-cam footage, and customers’ raw audio and video footage. The exposed data also included invoices of the company’s customers, which include police departments and prosecutors’ offices.

According to Anurag Sen, a good faith security researcher who found the data, the files were located on an Amazon-hosted (S3) cloud server that was openly listed and accessible to anyone via an easy-to-guess web address — no passwords needed.

The security lapse underscores how simple flaws or misconfigurations can result in sensitive information getting exposed online, especially as AI makes it easier to uncover weaknesses that can put companies and their data at risk.

Sen discovered the exposed data online in October and alerted the company to the issue, but did not hear back. Sen later provided details to TechCrunch in an effort to flag the incident with the company for resolution.

Sen, 30, is no stranger to TechCrunch. For the past decade, he has searched for sensitive datasets exposed online with the goal of notifying the companies and organizations that their information is open to the internet. Like many security researchers, much of his efforts are driven by a duty to secure the internet, and he describes his work as an “unpaid air-traffic controller.”

From his island home in Indonesia, Sen has uncovered sensitive U.S. military emails spilling from a compartmentalized Department of Defense cloud server; databases exposing reams of customer records; the inner workings of a country’s national license plate surveillance system; and public systems that inadvertently sent out streams of SMS codes used by people around the world to log into their online accounts.

Given Sen’s propensity for finding often highly confidential information online, we verified the source of the leak and the data, and contacted Tigerfish.

Soon after making contact, Tigerfish secured its exposed S3 cloud bucket.

“We’ve blocked all public access to the bucket you identified, including directory listings and individual files,” Tigerfish president, Adam Goldberg, said in an email. “We’ve also verified that all of our other S3 buckets are blocked to public access.”

“We’re continuing to review and strengthen our storage security more broadly,” added Goldberg.

The company said that Sen’s email disclosing the data leak was caught in its spam filter.

It’s unclear if the company has notified its customers. Tigerfish did not respond to a follow-up email.

“Basic human error”

Discoveries of exposed datasets have consumed a large part of Sen’s early cybersecurity career so far. He scours the web daily using automated scanners and specialist search engines to identify databases, cloud storage, or other sensitive information that likely shouldn’t be left unprotected online.

The modern web runs on absolute trust, he said, and operates under the notion that the world’s data is kept secure. But he described how his findings reveal the reality of how “fragile” the internet is behind the scenes.

Despite the recent focus on how AI is accelerating people’s ability to discover vulnerabilities, Sen said that many of the data leaks and exposures that he finds come down to basic human errors.

“An engineer spinning up a test cloud database on a Friday, disabling authentication to test an API, and forgetting to shut the door before heading into the weekend,” was just one example, he recounted.

title: If you missed the confirmation yesterday, here's what J. P. Morgan had to say about its most recent data breach on X:"Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses."    "There is no disruption to our services."More:Infosecurity-Magazine: JPMorgan Confirms Customer Data Breach Following Third-Party Compromise https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/jpmorgan-data-breach-third-party/ #infosec #databreach #cyberattack
text:
Written by

James CokerDeputy Editor, Infosecurity MagazineFollow @ReporterCoker

JPMorgan has confirmed a data breach following a cyber-attack on third party vendors used by the financial institution.

The investment banking giant, part of the JPMorganChase group, revealed on X on November 19, at 13.29 GMT, that it believes attackers accessed certain marketing data held by the impacted vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses.

“There is no disruption to our services. Where appropriate, we will contact affected customers directly and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring,” JPMorgan wrote.

The firm added that the incident is not related to a service disruption on November 16, which it said was caused by a software bug in its on-premise hardware systems.

Chase, which is the consumer and retail banking arm of JPMorganChase, issued the same statement on its X account on November 19.

N0n Ransomware Claims Attacks on JPMorgan, Visa and Mastercard

The notification came after the ransomware group N0n listed the financial institutions JPMorganChase, Visa and Mastercard on its data leak site.

Reuters reported that Visa and Mastercard confirmed they had experienced data breaches as a result of a third-party compromise. Visa said that no payment data has been impacted while a Mastercard spokesperson revealed that the breach affected non-payments information from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program.

None of the compromised third-party vendors have been named, so it is unknown at the time of writing if the incidents are related.

Following JPMorgan’s data breach notification on November 19, N0n reportedly released data relating to customers of the three banks, stating that they had each missed a 48-hour deadline to pay its extortion demand.
N0n group’s claim to have leaked data from JPMorganChase, Visa and Mastercard. Source: HackRisk.io
According to a report by the Wall Street Journal, personal data from thousands of customers from the three financial organizations were included in the leak. This includes 16,000 customer email addresses linked to JPMorgan’s invitation-only Reserve card program, typically reserved for clients with $10m or more in managed assets.

Rafe Pilling, senior director of threat intelligence, Sophos Counter Threat Unit, cautioned that the N0n group is having a “real impact” but some of its claims around major brands need to be treated with caution.

“In several cases, the data appears to have come from third-party providers running marketing, loyalty or concierge programs, rather than from the brands’ own networks,” he explained. “That still matters to the individuals whose data has been exposed, but it’s very different from saying criminals have broken into Visa or JPMorgan and are moving around inside their systems.”

N0n is a relatively new ransomware group, first observed in September 2026. The actor has reportedly threatened victims with destroying their backup infrastructure if they do not give in and pay its extortion demand.

title: UK operation wards off risk of cyber-attack on supermarket fridges and freezers
text: Empty fresh food refrigerators at an Intermarché supermarket in Névez, western France, in October, following a cyber-attack affecting the French supermarket chains. Photograph: Fred Tanneau/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEmpty fresh food refrigerators at an Intermarché supermarket in Névez, western France, in October, following a cyber-attack affecting the French supermarket chains. Photograph: Fred Tanneau/AFP/Getty Images UK operation wards off risk of cyber-attack on supermarket fridges and freezersNews of vulnerability comes after retailers in at least seven European countries hit by cyber-attacks A secret government cybersecurity operation recently warded off the risk of a cyber-attack on fridges and freezers in UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums, it has emerged.An attack would have been similar to those that have caused many millions of euros of damage in continental Europe in recent months. But, while many retailers have now been protected, researchers warned that many more could still be vulnerable.News of the operation led by Whitehall and the National Cyber Security Centre, first reported by the BBC, follows a cyberattack this month of supermarket chains in at least seven European countries.Another wave of attacks also affected hundreds of retailers across France in October in an act of “unprecedented scale and unprecedented aggression” for which Paris has publicly blamed Iran. The Pentagon is also investigating a suspected hack after a series of fridge malfunctions hit at least six US military bases in August.The French fridge hacks were relatively unsophisticated. An AI-enabled attack would raise the stakesRead moreExperts told the Guardian that if the vulnerability in UK-based devices had been discovered and exploited before a fix was found, the consequences would have been serious.“This incident should serve as a wake-up call for the entire refrigeration industry,” said Garry Turner-Smith of Omega Solutions, a refrigeration consultancy firm whose employee, Neil McCourt, found the vulnerability in devices manufactured by Resource Data Management (RDM).He said: “Had these weaknesses been discovered and exploited by someone with malicious intentions, they could have gained full control of vulnerable RDM data managers and used that access to interfere with refrigeration systems across multiple sites. This raises the prospect of attacks similar to those seen in Europe.”After Omega was alerted to the weakness, the firm called in the cybersecurity consultants Pen Test Partners to investigate. Both firms then raised their concerns with the manufacturer, RDM.Ken Munro, Pen Test Partners’ managing partner, said: “We determined that there was an urgent requirement to alert supermarkets and the food supply chain to the issue and fix. “However, we also had to work quietly to avoid alerting less ethical hackers and nation states of the likes of Iran, who are active in this space.”Munro was attending a retail industry cyber event the day the vulnerabilities were found, enabling him to meet National Cyber Security Centre representatives in person to share the intelligence.That triggered a series of briefing calls between retailers and officials from the National Cyber Security Centre, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs and the Food Standards Agency, among others, Munro said.Who is hacking Europe’s supermarket fridges and freezers, and why? title: ‘Russophobia’: a narrative for every occasion
text:
Disinformation Review

‘Russophobia’: a narrative for every occasion

By EUvsDisinfo | November 20, 2026

Key Takeaways

The Kremlin uses ‘Russophobia’ as an all-purpose narrative to dismiss evidence of Russian interference, discredit Western governments, justify claims of escalation and corruption, and portray the countries most exposed to Russian pressure as irrationally hostile to Moscow.

Note: This section is auto-generated based on the article content.

‘Russophobia’: a narrative for every occasion

➕ Add to Playlist

Please rate your listening experience

The Kremlin uses ‘Russophobia’ as an all-purpose narrative to dismiss evidence of Russian interference, discredit Western governments, justify claims of escalation and corruption, and portray the countries most exposed to Russian pressure as irrationally hostile to Moscow.
On 15 November, Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna announced that Estonia would close all checkpoints(opens in a new tab) on its border with Russia from 1 December. The move followed what Estonian authorities described as clear evidence that Russia’s military intelligence service, the GRU, had ordered a sabotage attack against an Estonian defence company. A day earlier, Estonia had detained eight Latvian citizens suspected of acting on Russian instructions and planning an arson or explosive attack against the Threod Systems drone factory in Viimsi, near Tallinn.
Caught out? Cry ‘Russophobia’
Russia responded with a familiar routine. First came denial: Moscow claimed that the detained Latvians had nothing to do with the alleged sabotage and that Estonia had provided no proof. Then came the inevitable blame-shifting. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova said that, if Tallinn really intended to close the border, the decision would fit into ‘yet another bout of aggressive and unrestrained Russophobia’.
Claiming ‘Russophobia’ – an irrational fear or dislike of Russia or Russians – may be one of the Kremlin’s most useful inventions. It’s a wonderfully versatile narrative: whenever Moscow has no convincing answer to accusations or evidence of Russian interference, it can declare them ‘Russophobic’ without addressing the matter further.
One narrative, many uses
The wider Russophobia narrative comes with its own set of useful subplots. One is distinctly anti-elite: ordinary Europeans are supposedly not hostile to Russia, but are being manipulated(opens in a new tab) by politicians and the media into being ‘Russophobic’. Implying deliberate manipulation by governments is useful enough on its own for encouraging distrust in public institutions, and from there, the narrative is easily expanded further: if politicians are manufacturing Russophobia, they must be doing it for a reason.
One convenient explanation is money. Russophobia can supposedly be used to justify higher military spending – naturally, followed by corruption. A recent RIA Novosti article followed exactly this logic(opens in a new tab), claiming that British authorities had made Russophobia profitable by inventing Russian spy threats and then introducing a new tax to pay for the response.
Russophobia can also be presented as a pretext for escalation. Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov recently made that connection(opens in a new tab), claiming that the West had turned Russophobia into ‘a hot commodity’ and ‘a driver of militarisation’, while openly preparing for a possible conflict with Russia. At this point, one major Kremlin narrative neatly merges with another: Russophobia becomes proof of the ‘warmongering West’.
Another supposed benefit is political distraction. According to pro-Kremlin outlets, Western leaders exaggerate the Russian threat because it helps them hide their failures at home(opens in a new tab). This fits neatly into the familiar ‘decaying West’ narrative: governments unable to solve domestic problems supposedly need an external enemy to keep their citizens looking elsewhere.

title: Première historique : le Myanmar condamné pour génocide

Première historique : le Myanmar condamné pour génocide

1 min. de lecture

Citer

Partager

Imprimeren PDF

Ajouter aux favoris

Pascal Boniface

Directeur de l’IRIS

Le jeudi 19 novembre, la Cour internationale de justice (CIJ) a reconnu que le Myanmar avait commis un génocide contre la minorité rohingya. Une décision historique : pour la première fois, la Cour établit la responsabilité d’un État pour génocide.

Les faits remontent notamment aux opérations militaires de 2017, qui ont fait plus de 10 000 morts et poussé plus de 700 000 Rohingyas à fuir vers le Bangladesh. Aujourd’hui, plus de 1,2 million de Rohingyas y sont réfugiés, notamment dans les camps de Cox’s Bazar.

La procédure avait été engagée en novembre 2019 par la Gambie, avec le soutien de l’Organisation de la coopération islamique (OCI). Au-delà de la reconnaissance du génocide, ce jugement constitue un précédent juridique majeur. Il pourrait notamment éclairer la procédure engagée par l’Afrique du Sud contre Israël, en particulier sur la question de l’intention génocidaire et l’appréciation des preuves.

Mais cette avancée intervient dans un contexte de fortes pressions sur les institutions judiciaires internationales. Le 22 octobre, l’ambassadeur américain à l’ONU, Mike Waltz, s’en est pris publiquement à Navanethem Pillay, juge ad hoc dans cette affaire, l’accusant de vouloir abaisser le seuil juridique de reconnaissance du génocide. Une nouvelle illustration des attaques visant les instances du droit international.

Mon analyse dans cette vidéo.

title: Co-Creating the New Europe: The Road, Not the Destination in EU–UK Talks
text: European safety: Ursula von der Leyen announcing the €35 billion loan from the EU to Ukraine, secured by future profits from frozen Russian assets. Image: Sipa US / Alamy StockAs leaders meet in Brussels on 20 November, a more useful question than re-joining the EU is what the UK will help to build next.When Prime Minister Andy Burnham meets António Costa and Ursula von der Leyen in Brussels on 20 November, the discussion in Westminster will already have a frame. Politicians and officials ask how, or whether, the UK could rejoin. This commentary argues against that frame in four steps. The EU that Britain left no longer exists, and the Europe of 2028 or 2030 will differ again from today's, which makes the task one of joint construction. The effort to anchor Ukraine in Europe and preserve peace on the continent is pushing the EU to invent new formats of association, and that widens the options open to the UK. Britain's weight in Ukraine's security places it inside this work, with the E3 (France, Germany and the UK) as its core. And the summit will absorb much of its energy in money and procedure, so both sides need to protect the strategic track that runs alongside.A Destination That Keeps MovingTalk of ‘rejoining’ assumes a fixed address to which one returns, but the EU has moved. It has opened accession negotiations with Ukraine and Moldova. It has put together a €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan and a €150 billion defence lending instrument (Security Action for Europe, or SAFE). NATO's July report puts the defence spending of European Allies and Canada at about $634 billion for 2026 at constant 2021 prices, a real increase of nearly 11% in a year, and Germany now spends more than the UK in absolute terms after radically changing its doctrine. An organisation that is adding members, creating categories and financing defence at this scale will look different as soon as one or two years from now. Focusing on the end risks distracting from the importance of the road that needs to be travelled. The question of return has no stable reference point; what London and Brussels can do on 20 November is take part in drawing the next one.quoteKyiv is unlikely to sign a settlement that leaves it outside European structures in practice, so integration has to become tangible well before accession is complete Ukraine as the Organising QuestionEuropean capitals share the view that a lasting peace needs Ukraine anchored in the continent, in security terms and well beyond them. The negotiations bring the point home. Whatever settlement is finally reached, it falls on Europe to provide the conditions to make it stick and avoid a toxic peace that could further undermine everyone’s security. Russian officials want a broad agreement on Europe's security architecture, and US negotiator Jared Kushner said in Moscow on 12 November that he had begun discussing it with European partners.
