title: Beyond the Menu – Pragmatism over Purity in UK–EU Relations
text: Britain's Prime Minister Andy Burnham, European Council President Antonio Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen during the visit for the EU-UK summit in Brussels, Belgium, Friday Nov. 20, 2026.At the UK–EU Summit on 20 November, both sides should drop Brexit-era red lines and fixed institutional models in favour of pragmatic cooperation built on shared interests.In the months preceding the UK–EU Summit on 20 November, the old guard on both sides of the Channel emerged to offer their opinions on the future relationship. Chief among these were two men present at the destruction: former EU Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier and former UK Prime Minister David Cameron. While Barnier warned that the UK must not be allowed to ‘cherry pick’ in seeking to rejoin the EU internal market, Cameron cautioned that any effort to rejoin the bloc would be ‘very long and painful’. For years, the EU has presented the UK the same trio of available institutional arrangements – namely a customs union, joining the single market or full membership – rather than entertaining any flexibility or deviations from this menu fixe.While a purist, one-size-fits-all approach was feasible in a relatively benign security environment underpinned by US security guarantees, it is ill-suited to today’s more volatile, less predictable geopolitical environment in which the US is reducing its contributions to transatlantic security. To increase its leverage and influence globally, the EU needs to join forces with willing, capable and like-minded countries. This means shedding the shared trauma of Brexit and adopting a more flexible approach to the future relationship with the UK, with its £3 trillion economy and significant defence assets. Public opinion supports this direction of travel. A June 2026 European Council on Foreign Relations poll revealed that three-quarters of Britons support a closer relationship with the EU while EU voters are also positively inclined toward a closer relationship with the UK.quoteMutual recognition may be a better path than full alignment, with the EU even choosing to adopt elements of the UK regulatory approach, and vice versa, as best practices emerge. Differentiation is already accepted practice within the EU As UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham and his EU counterparts advance the UK–EU relationship at Summit on 20 November, the politicians and civil servants steering the process would do well to adhere to several guiding principles to gain momentum and maintain public support for even more ambitious cooperation in future.Focus on Substance, Not StructureMost importantly, the UK and EU should not fixate on the specific institutional arrangements. Rather, they need to focus on the substance and begin by defining common interests and challenges as well as the results they want to achieve. These might include spurring growth, lowering energy prices, protecting critical infrastructure, building supply chain resilience or increasing defence production and innovation. BADBOX 3.0 malware used Android TV boxes to generate 40 billion daily bid requests
November 20, 2026 By Bill Mann — Leave a Comment XLinkedInRedditFacebook

HUMAN Security says it disrupted BADBOX 3.0, an ad fraud operation that used compromised streaming boxes to play hidden video ads and sell access to their owners’ home internet connections.

At its peak, the operation generated roughly 40 billion requests a day, inviting advertisers to bid for ad placements.

That was more than triple the volume of the previous record holder, VASTFLUX, and accounted for more than 4% of the connected TV ad traffic HUMAN monitored at the time. HUMAN called it the largest publicly disclosed ad fraud operation by bid volume.

HUMAN

HUMAN’s Satori team traced the operation to a backdoor packaged as a system app. The backdoor fetched fraud modules from public code repositories, where researchers found tools from earlier BADBOX campaigns alongside new ones. By mid-2026, the team had spotted a surge in ad requests claiming to come from a legitimate streaming app.

The affected hardware consisted mainly of inexpensive, off-brand streaming boxes made in China and sold internationally. They ran versions of the Android Open Source Project without Google Play Protect certification. Satori linked the malware catalog to Chinese electronics manufacturer TXCZ, citing a company domain that hosted payloads and supplied hidden-ad settings, as well as modules that checked for TXCZ-specific device properties.

The malware played video ads outside the visible screen while sending requests that impersonated legitimate streaming apps. To advertisers, the requests looked like opportunities to reach viewers using familiar apps on home internet connections. In one impersonated app’s case, about 80% of US requests came from IP addresses that researchers flagged as residential proxy exits.

HUMAN also found fabricated requests that claimed a streaming service had inserted an ad into a viewer’s stream. In those cases, the supposed viewer device did not exist, and no ad played.

The same malware catalog could enroll compromised boxes in any of 11 residential proxy networks without the owners’ consent. Those services let customers route traffic through someone else’s home connection, using the owner’s bandwidth and public IP address. Ten networks were commercially available. HUMAN says the eleventh, PXYEDGE, is a rebrand of IpMoYu, a proxy network the BADBOX operators ran in the previous campaign.

HUMAN

A separate Google-led takedown of the XCPE botnet also hit several domains that controlled parts of BADBOX 3.0, according to HUMAN. Google said XCPE had enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes.

HUMAN recommends buying streaming boxes from established brands and using official app stores. If your box has the Google Play Store, check its certification under Profile → Settings → About. Google also maintains a list of certified devices through the store.

Fresh security updates for the Ruby programming language resolve seven vulnerabilities in its regular expression engine and in the case conversion of strings. Proof-of-concept (PoC) code demonstrating remote code execution (RCE) exists for five of them.

At the top of the list sits CVE-2026-132825 (CVSS score of 7.4), described as a heap-based buffer overflow in the case conversion of strings that could potentially lead to RCE in certain scenarios.

Dubbed Ruby2Shell, the flaw impacts character case-conversion operations. In some single-byte encodings, including ISO-8859-1 and Windows-1252, when changing the case of a string, Ruby may end up writing one byte past the output buffer.

“For example, converting the German character ß to uppercase produces SS. In affected code, Ruby checks that sufficient space exists for one byte but writes two, potentially corrupting adjacent heap memory,” Previdian explains.

Veria Labs reports that, in default Ruby configurations, unauthenticated attackers could trigger the security defect from Rails, classic-style Sinatra, and potentially other frameworks.

According to preemptive exposure management firm WatchTowr, “any Ruby application that changes the case of external text in a single-byte encoding” is affected by the vulnerability.

According to Veria Labs, which plans to release a PoC after major vendors have rolled out patches, GitHub Enterprise Server is affected. Chatwoot, GitLab, Mastodon, OpenProject, and the Discourse base image have patched the bug.

Successful exploitation of Ruby2Shell in production environments is likely to be challenging, WatchTowr principal threat intelligence specialist Yordan Ganchev told SecurityWeek.

According to him, correctly laying out memory is difficult, and “attackers would also need the right non-glibc memory allocator, runtime configuration, and application logic preconditions, making exploitation even more challenging.”

“And if that weren’t enough, they’d need to contend with anyone else hammering the system on the internet and, in the end, defeat Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), making the whole journey a complete odyssey,” Ganchev noted.

Most likely, malformed requests could lead to denial-of-service (DoS) and service disruption, he said.

The other four vulnerabilities with a PoC demonstrating RCE include a double free, two integer overflows, and a heap-based buffer overflow. CVE identifiers for these issues have been requested but not assigned yet. PoC code also exists for an out-of-bounds read, demonstrating memory corruption.

Ruby also resolved an out-of-bounds read in its regular expression engine that could lead to memory leaks and process crashes.

Patches for all seven vulnerabilities were included in Ruby versions 4.0.10, 3.4.13, or 3.3.14. Users are advised to apply the fixes as soon as possible.

After some early adopters of Meta’s Muse AI agent complained that it was spying on private messages and behaving unpredictably earlier this fall, Reuters exposed internal chats showing that Meta staff had raised the same alarms.
When testing the agent, staff warned that Muse appeared to be accessing encrypted private messages that users did not expect the bot to review, could be mixing up conversations between users, and even potentially sharing sensitive information users would never expect to be exposed.
Some unexpected Muse outputs responded to questions that staffers never asked.
“Hmmm,” one Meta staffer wrote in an instance where Muse sent the definition of “money laundering” unbidden. “Got a random ping from Muse about something I definitely did not ask for… .”
In at least one case, Muse told a staffer surprised by a similarly out-of-context offer to message a seller about a coffee table that it had “pulled in some context about a coffee table pickup that doesn’t seem to be yours.”
According to Reuters, that employee flagged the troubling output, writing, “this was ‘not my conversation’” and “expressing concern about a ‘possible cross-account context leak.’”
Raising the most concern were random outputs that appeared to share private user data. For example, a perplexed Meta staffer chatting with Muse about fishing got a random extra response, seemingly sharing balances from two unknown bank accounts. That output said, “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”
At least one staffer said they lost money testing Muse, Reuters reported. That staffer reported that Muse “accidentally rolled me into a premium insurance plan” for their dog that charged them $888 per month instead of their prior rate of $200. “Couldn’t recover,” the staffer said.

Meta’s spokesperson, Daniel Roberts, told Reuters that these were “isolated incidents,” and internally employees were told that “the agent appeared to be hallucinating messages in response to built-in prompts pushing it to engage with users in between sessions.” In those cases, an AI team member said the hallucinations were “unfortunately” biased “towards the most uncomfortable topics, like finances/security/safety, which sucks.” In some cases, instead of bank details, Muse hallucinated bitcoin balances, the team member said.
A Meta spokesperson told Ars that “employee testing is core to the product development process and the entire point is to get feedback, so we can implement safety and privacy protections and improve products. Importantly, employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.”
Speaking to Reuters, Roberts reiterated that “many of the messages flagged by employees as potential account mix-ups were hallucinations” that Meta had already addressed.
But Roberts declined to respond to Reuters’ questions on the prevalence or persistence of the issues the AI team member discussed. And Reuters’ report emphasized that the outlet independently was “unable to establish whether Muse was giving users other people’s bank account balances and other sensitive data, or making up the information.”
Muse issues arose soon after September launch
Meta started receiving privacy-related complaints from Muse users in September. An Inc. Magazine reporter, Jason Aten, was shocked when it became clear that Muse was digging through private messages on his Mac without permission, reporting that he instead “explicitly” chose to deny Muse that access. As Meta delayed responding, the agent claimed it was simply parsing text in push notifications, but Aten found that “wasn’t true.” Rather, the agent was syncing messages from a local database, which Aten said was activated without his knowledge.

British hackers face prison for GTA 6 data breach and crypto thefts

Zack Whittaker

6:55 AM PST · November 18, 2026

Two British hackers are facing lengthy prison sentences for separate hacks as part of their roles in long-running, prolific cybercriminal hacking groups. The two are accused of hacks that stole millions of dollars in cryptocurrency and leaked pre-release footage from Grand Theft Auto VI.

Tyler Buchanan, 24, from Dundee, Scotland, has been sentenced to six years by a U.S. court after he was extradited to the United States in 2025. Buchanan was accused of stealing at least $11 million in cryptocurrency from dozens of companies as part of a phishing scheme. The attacks would impersonate IT helpdesks and call up unsuspecting employees and trick them into giving over their credentials, which the hackers would use to break in and steal cryptocurrency.

Meanwhile, Arion Kurtaj, 21, from Oxford, England, has pleaded guilty to several cyberattacks that he carried out while a teenager. One hack included the theft of data and extortion of Rockstar Games, the maker of Grand Theft Auto VI, which was released Wednesday after several delays.

Kurtaj was previously ordered by a U.K. court to be detained indefinitely after deeming him unable to stand trial due to his autism diagnosis and his perceived high hacking risk to the public. But U.K. authorities, tasked with charging Kurtaj with cybercrime offenses, confirmed Monday that he had admitted to several hacks, including leaking footage of the long-awaited video game, and would subsequently face a public trial.

U.K. authorities confirmed earlier reporting that Kurtaj hacked several companies, including while he was confined to a hotel amid police protection from rival criminal gangs. The authorities said Kurtaj used an Amazon Fire TV stick to hack the companies, which breached his bail conditions.

Both Buchanan and Kurtaj were members of overlapping cybercriminal groups, dubbed 0ktapus, Lapsus$, and later Scattered Spider. These prolific hacking gangs mostly consist of teenagers and young male adults, lending to the term “advanced persistent teenagers,” whose focus and motivations were to steal as much money as possible through various cyberattacks.

Over the years, the hackers were collectively responsible for hundreds of cyberattacks targeting big companies, including Coinbase, DoorDash, Mailchimp, and Nvidia.

By late 2024, both U.K. and U.S. authorities say they had indicted five of the hackers whom they believed were key members of the hacking groups, including Buchanan. The U.S. Department of Justice said this week that Buchanan is the fifth and final defendant to be sentenced in this case.

Application DevelopmentSashiko: Lessons from building an agentic code review system for LinuxNovember 19, 2026Roman GushchinSoftware Engineer, AI & InfrastructureEric BrewerVP, Infrastructure & Google Fellow, AI & InfrastructureTry Gemini todayThe front door to AI in the workplaceTry now The speed of development in large open-source projects has always been limited by code review, not code generation. Even as coding agents get better at writing code, they do not accelerate development on their own. This is especially true of patches to the Linux kernel. Without a way to build trust in proposed changes, more generated code simply piles up in front of the same small group of human maintainers. Some of those patches are solid changes, just written faster; many others are plausible-looking "AI slop" sent by contributors who do not fully understand the systems they are modifying. And the influx of AI-generated security reports, many of which are duplicates or inaccurate, only adds to maintainers’ load.
Linux runs billions of Android phones, most cloud providers, and nearly every supercomputer. It spans more than 35 million lines of code, and over 85,000 changes land every year. Automated build bots and fuzzers like Syzkaller catch build errors and crashes, but code review has always been the main way to guarantee the stability and safety of the kernel. Every day, maintainers read hundreds and hundreds of proposed patches by hand to catch memory leaks, deadlocks, race conditions, and security bugs.To help maintainers handle the load and catch bugs before they land, the Google AI & Infrastructure team built Sashiko, an open-source, agentic code review system powered by Gemini. We named the project after the Japanese word 刺し子, a stitching technique for artistically reinforcing worn cloth, and donated it to the Linux Foundation earlier this year.In this blog, we cover the problem Sashiko was designed to solve, how it works, what the data shows, and what we learned from building and running it in the wild.Reviewing code is hardReviewing a change in a complex code base is objectively hard, both for humans and LLMs. It often requires a deep understanding of how the system works in general, well outside the proposed change. In fact, it’s pretty common to see patches that engineers claim perfectly solve the problem, but if they were to be merged, would actually introduce even worse problems (albeit subtle). Traditionally, only experienced maintainers have been able to spot and prevent these issues. The same is true for agentically generated code.To verify the correctness of a change, a potentially large number of invariants should be proven, which is often a much larger and harder task than developing the change itself. This is true for both human and agentic reviewers. However, LLM-based reviewers have some unique properties, both positive and negative:LLMs often struggle to put in enough effort. LLMs are trained to achieve the goal of spending fewer tokens. So they often tend to cut corners and dismiss concerns without proper investigation or flag false positives without proper due diligence.LLMs are easier to bias. The current generation of LLMs usually performs much better if provided a single relatively simple task (e.g., prove the patch for memory leaks) rather than multiple tasks (e.g., explore several complex, varied concerns). It’s pretty common for an LLM to find an obvious issue in the code and refuse to look deeper for other types of issues. Also, commit log text can sometimes affect the result of code review in a non-predicatable or even malicious way.LLMs don’t have persistent memory. Surprisingly, this is a positive thing for code review: An LLM can review the same or similar patch multiple times as if it were a new patch. Introducing agent controls: An enterprise control plane for agent behavior
A managed Azure service, agent controls brings runtime policy to enterprise agents, built on the open-source Agent Control Specification (ACS) and Agent Hooks.
By Mehrnoosh SamekiPrincipal PM Manager, Microsoft, Mohamed ElmergawiPrincipal Software Engineering Manager, Microsoft, Mike ShiTechnical Program Manager, Microsoft, Liam CrummSenior Software Engineer, Microsoft, and Responsible AI at MicrosoftMicrosoft’s Responsible AI team
2026.11.18

Today, we’re introducing agent controls, a managed Azure service that helps enterprises centrally define, manage, and evaluate policies governing AI agent behavior across frameworks, platforms, and clouds.

Built on the open-source Agent Control Specification (ACS) and Agent Hooks, agent controls brings runtime governance to enterprise AI agents without requiring organizations to build and operate their own policy evaluation infrastructure.

As enterprises deploy agents across different frameworks and environments, governance becomes increasingly fragmented. Each application team may implement its own policies, enforcement integrations, and monitoring, creating inconsistent controls and increasing operational complexity. Enterprises need a unified way to govern agent behavior without rebuilding governance infrastructure for every application.

Why agent controls

As enterprises move from experimenting with AI agents to running them at scale, one question starts to dominate every deployment review: how do you make thousands of autonomous agents follow your organization’s policies, no matter who built them, what framework they run on, or which cloud they live in?

For a fleet of AI agents to remain safe and secure, governance has to cover not only what an agent says, but also what it does. And a safe answer isn’t a safe action: an agent can produce a perfectly appropriate response and still move money it shouldn’t, call a tool it isn’t authorized to use, or send data somewhere it doesn’t belong.

We started by making this governance open. Runtime control only works if a policy can follow an agent wherever it runs, and that’s impossible if every framework and vendor invents its own way to intervene and decide. So we open-sourced the two primitives underneath agent controls, Agent Hooks and the Agent Control Specification (ACS), as a community-driven, inspectable contract, with the goal of setting a shared market standard for runtime agent governance that any runtime, framework, or safety provider can adopt. A policy written once should be portable everywhere:

Agent Hooks defines where control happens. It creates a common set of intervention points across the agent lifecycle, including startup, input, model calls, tool calls, output, and shutdown. The runtime pauses at each point and asks for a decision.

The Agent Control Specification (ACS) defines how the decision is made. ACS is an open request-and-decision contract. At each hook, ACS gathers evidence through annotators (safety classifiers, LLM judges, deterministic business rules, or any external API) and passes it to a policy engine such as Rego, which returns the decision.

Open primitives solve portability, but not operations. In our conversations with enterprise customers, the same five requirements come up again and again:

Central governance without taking away developer flexibility: Security and IT need to set organization-wide policy once. Developers need to keep building on their preferred frameworks, models, and clouds. Neither should have to give up what they need to satisfy the other.

Enforcement at runtime, not guidance in a prompt: A policy that lives in a system prompt is a suggestion. Enterprises need agent behavior evaluated and controlled at the decision points that matter, before data is shared, before a tool runs, before a consequential action is taken.
